options: D1, D2, D3 and the horizon price P3 = D4/(R − g)
D1, D2, D3, D4 and the horizon price P3 = D4/(R − g)
D1, D2, D3 and the horizon price P4 = D5/(R − g)
D1, D2 and the horizon price P2 = D3/(R − g)
questions.explanation: Constant growth starts with D4, so the horizon price is P3 = D4/(R − g) and it already contains D4 and every later dividend. Adding D4 separately double-counts it. Moving the horizon to P4 or P2 puts the formula one period away from the first constant-growth dividend.

questions.stem: Nova Cedar Mills pays no dividend for three years. Its first dividend, D4 = $0.90, is followed by growth of 7% per year forever, and R = 12% per annum. What is the correct first computation?
options: P4 = D4/(R − g) = $18.00, a value at the end of year 4
P3 = D4(1 + g)/(R − g) = $19.26, a value at the end of year 3
P0 = D4/(R − g) = $18.00, because the formula gives today's price
P3 = D4/(R − g) = 0.90/(0.12 − 0.07) = $18.00, a value at the end of year 3
questions.explanation: D4 is already the first constant-growth dividend, so it goes straight into the numerator: 0.90/0.05 = $18.00, valued one period earlier, at year 3. Multiplying by (1 + g) again ($19.26) grows the dividend twice; labelling the result P4 or P0 puts the date in the wrong place.

questions.stem: How does valuing a non-constant-growth stock differ from applying the Gordon model at date 0?
options: Non-constant growth ignores the irregular early dividends and values only the horizon price at date T
Non-constant growth uses a different required return for every year of the early irregular phase
Non-constant growth uses the supernormal rate g1 in the horizon-price formula, where Gordon uses g2
Gordon values the whole stream at date 0 from D1; non-constant growth applies the formula at date T and discounts back
questions.explanation: Gordon needs one constant g from the very first dividend. When growth changes, the formula only works from the date constant growth begins, so we value the stock there (P_T), then pull P_T and the earlier dividends back with (1 + R)^t. The horizon price uses g2, the long-run rate, never g1.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the standard non-constant growth procedure?
options: Listing the explicit dividends through date T on a timeline of the cash flows
Growing D_T by the supernormal rate g1 to obtain D_{T+1} for the horizon price
Finding the date of the first dividend that grows at the constant rate
Discounting the horizon price back T periods to date 0 along with the dividends
questions.explanation: D_{T+1} is the first dividend of the constant-growth phase, so it is D_T grown at g2, not g1 (horizon-wrong-g). The other three statements are the real steps: timeline, locate the first constant-growth dividend, discount P_T together with the early dividends.

questions.stem: Why can the first-phase growth rate g1 exceed the required return R, while the long-run rate g2 cannot?
options: Investors apply a lower discount rate to the dividends of the first phase than to later dividends
g1 is a growth rate of earnings per share, while g2 is a growth rate of dividends per share
The Gordon formula only requires g2 to be positive; it does not need to be smaller than R
The first phase has finitely many dividends, so its value is finite; the infinite phase needs g2 < R for P = D/(R − g2)
questions.explanation: A finite stream of fast-growing dividends always has a finite value, even when g1 > R. An infinite stream growing at g2 ≥ R would have an infinite or negative value from the formula, which is why the long-run rate must stay below R (SM 8-30 stock Y).

questions.stem: Put the steps of a non-constant growth valuation in the correct order.
options: Timeline and dividends → D_{T+1} → P_T = D_{T+1}/(R − g2) → discount everything to date 0 and add
Discount the explicit dividends → P_T = D_{T+1}/(R − g2) → find D_{T+1} → add the discounted amounts
P_T = D_{T+1}/(R − g2) → timeline and explicit dividends → discount to date 0 → find D_{T+1}
First constant-growth dividend D_{T+1} → discount to date 0 → P_T = D_{T+1}/(R − g2) → timeline
questions.explanation: You cannot compute P_T until you know which dividend starts constant growth and when it is paid, and you cannot add anything until every piece is a date-0 value. So: timeline, D_{T+1}, horizon price, discount and sum.

questions.stem: True or false: if the first constant-growth dividend is D6, the horizon price is P5 = D6/(R − g2).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The Gordon formula values the stock one period before the dividend in its numerator, so D6 gives P5. Then P5 is discounted five periods (not six).

questions.stem: A student values a stock whose dividend growth is 18% for five years and 4% thereafter, with R = 12%. Her horizon-price step returns a NEGATIVE number. The most likely cause is that she:
options: discounted the horizon price one period too many before adding it to the dividends
used the first-phase rate g1 = 18% in R − g, which gives 12% − 18% = −6%
forgot to add the dividends of the first phase to the discounted horizon price
put D5 instead of D6 in the numerator of the Gordon formula
questions.explanation: A negative price from the Gordon formula means R − g < 0, so a growth rate above R was used. The horizon price must use g2 = 4%. The other slips change the size of the answer but cannot flip its sign.

questions.stem: Cobalt Peak Software will pay its first dividend, $2.40, at the end of year 7. Dividends then grow 6% per year forever and R = 13% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: The first dividend is D7, so P6 = 2.40/(0.13 − 0.06) = $34.2857. Discount six years: 34.2857/1.13^6 = $16.47. Discounting seven years ($14.57) treats P6 as a year-7 value; growing D7 once more ($17.46) double-counts a growth step; discounting five years ($18.61) places the horizon too early.

questions.stem: Tamarack Solar will pay $1.20, $1.80 and $2.40 at the ends of years 1, 2 and 3. From year 4 the dividend grows 4% per year forever (D4 = D3 × 1.04). R = 11% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: D4 = 2.40 × 1.04 = 2.496, so P3 = 2.496/0.07 = $35.6571. P0 = 1.20/1.11 + 1.80/1.11² + 2.40/1.11³ + 35.6571/1.11³ = 1.0811 + 1.4609 + 1.7549 + 26.0722 = $30.37. Dropping the three dividends gives $26.07; using D3 instead of D4 in the horizon price gives $29.37; discounting P3 four years gives $27.79.

questions.stem: Trillium Trucking just paid a dividend of $1.60. Dividends will grow 25% next year, 18% the year after, 12% in year 3, and 4% per year from year 4 onward. R = 11% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: D1 = 2.0000, D2 = 2.3600, D3 = 2.6432; D4 = D3 × 1.04 = 2.7489 grows at the LONG-RUN 4%, so P3 = 2.7489/0.07 = $39.27. P0 = 1.8018 + 1.9154 + 1.9327 + 28.7142 = $34.36. Growing D4 at 12% (the year-3 rate) inflates the price to $36.57; using D3 in the numerator gives $33.26; discounting P3 four years gives $31.52.

questions.stem: Peace River Foods pays no dividend for the next eight years. Its first dividend, D9 = $4.75, is paid at the end of year 9 and then grows 5.5% per year forever. R = 12.5% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)
solution: No dividends in years 1-8, first dividend D9 = $4.75 at the end of year 9, so the horizon is year 8.

errors.label: Discounted P8 for nine years
errors.explain: P8 is a year-8 value (one period before D9), so it is discounted eight periods, not nine.

errors.label: Grew D9 once more before dividing
errors.explain: D9 is already the first constant-growth dividend; multiplying by (1 + g) double-counts a growth step.

errors.label: Added g to R in the denominator
errors.explain: The denominator is R minus g.

questions.explanation: No dividends before year 9, so the Gordon formula applied to D9 gives the year-8 value, which is then discounted eight periods. Discounting nine periods is the classic horizon-off-by-one error.

questions.stem: Kootenay Kayaks will pay $0.60, $1.10 and $1.55 at the ends of years 1, 2 and 3. From year 4 the dividend grows 6% per year forever. R = 10.5% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)
solution: Constant growth starts with D4, so the horizon is year 3.

errors.label: Left out the year-1 dividend
errors.explain: Every dividend before the horizon is a separate cash flow; the horizon price does not include D1-D3.

errors.label: Used D3 in the horizon numerator
errors.explain: The horizon price needs the first constant-growth dividend D4 = D3(1.06), not D3.

errors.label: Discounted P3 four years
errors.explain: P3 is a year-3 value, so it is discounted three periods.

questions.explanation: Value the stock at year 3 with D4 in the numerator, discount that price and the three early dividends back, and add. The horizon price is by far the largest piece (about 91% of the total).

questions.stem: Nova Cedar Mills pays nothing in years 1 and 2, then $0.90 at the end of year 3 and $1.40 at the end of year 4. From year 5 the dividend grows 5% per year forever. R = 12% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: PV of the year-4 dividend plus P4

solution: Constant growth begins with D5, so the horizon is year 4 and both D3 and D4 are explicit.

errors.label: Used D4 instead of D5 in the horizon numerator
errors.explain: D4 is the last irregular dividend, not the first constant-growth dividend; the numerator for P4 must be D5 = D4 × 1.05.

errors.label: Dropped the year-4 dividend
errors.explain: D4 is an explicit dividend; P4 values only the dividends from year 5 onward.

errors.label: Discounted both year-4 amounts five years
errors.explain: The year-4 dividend and P4 are both year-4 values: discount four periods.

questions.explanation: Zeros in the early years are still part of the timeline. The key step is spotting that constant growth starts with D5, which puts the horizon at year 4 (the last irregular dividend D4 is paid with it).

questions.stem: Bow Valley Utilities will pay $0.85, $1.25 and $1.70 at the ends of years 1, 2 and 3. From year 4 the dividend grows 3.5% per year forever. R = 9.5% per annum. What price do you expect the stock to trade at at the end of year 2, just after that year's dividend is paid? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: Price at year 2: P2 = (D3 + P3)/(1 + R)

solution: At year 2 the only remaining cash flows are D3 and P3, one period away:

errors.label: Left out D3 and discounted only P3
errors.explain: The holder at year 2 still receives D3 at year 3, so D3 belongs with P3.

errors.label: Discounted P3 two years
errors.explain: From year 2 the horizon is only one period away, so P3 is discounted ONE period, not two.

errors.label: Added D2 to the year-2 price
errors.explain: D2 is paid at year 2; the ex-dividend price after payment excludes it, and D3 and P3 are discounted one period.

questions.explanation: A price at any date is the PV, at that date, of everything still to come. At year 2 that is D3 plus P3 discounted a single period.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Brewing will pay $0.95 and $1.40 at the ends of years 1 and 2. From year 3 the dividend grows 5% per year forever. R = 10% per annum. What percentage of today's price comes from the horizon price? (Answer in %.)

steps.label: Share of P0 from the horizon price (%)

errors.label: Used the undiscounted horizon price P2
errors.explain: P2 is a year-2 value; it must be discounted to date 0 before comparing it with today's price.

errors.label: Gave the share of the early dividends instead
errors.explain: That is the complement: the share of P0 that comes from the early dividends (about 8%).

questions.explanation: Most of the price of a growth stock sits in the horizon price. Here 92% of today's value is the discounted P2, so small errors in g2 or R matter far more than errors in the early dividends.

questions.stem: In the two-stage dividend formula P0 = D1/(R − g1) × [1 − ((1 + g1)/(1 + R))^N] + P_N/(1 + R)^N, the first term is:
options: the present value of the horizon price P_N
the present value of the N dividends that grow at g1 (a growing annuity)
the price at date N, just after the last supernormal dividend
the present value of a perpetuity growing at g1 forever
questions.explanation: The bracketed first term is the growing-annuity formula: it values only the N dividends D1 through D_N that grow at g1. Everything after year N is captured by the second term, the discounted horizon price P_N.

questions.stem: Which situation should be valued with the two-stage formula rather than the plain Gordon model?
options: Dividends grow 3% per year from now on, forever
The dividend stays at $2.00 per share every year, forever
The firm pays no dividend and is valued from a peer's P/E ratio
Dividends grow 18% per year for 6 years and then 4% per year forever
questions.explanation: Two-stage growth means one growth rate g1 for a fixed number of years, then a lower constant g2 forever. Constant growth is Gordon, a flat dividend is a perpetuity, and a P/E valuation is a comparables method.

questions.stem: In the two-stage formula, which growth rate appears in the denominator of the horizon price P_N, and which dividend is in its numerator?
options: g1, the first-stage rate, with D_N = D0(1 + g1)^N
g2, the long-run rate, with D_N = D0(1 + g1)^N
g1, the first-stage rate, with D_{N+1} = D0(1 + g1)^N(1 + g2)
g2, the long-run rate, with D_{N+1} = D0(1 + g1)^N(1 + g2)
questions.explanation: P_N values the dividends from N+1 onward, which grow at g2 forever, so it uses R − g2 and the first dividend of that stream, D_{N+1}. D_{N+1} is D_N (grown N times at g1) grown ONE more step at g2.

questions.stem: A start-up's dividend growth is expected to be 30% per year for 5 years and then 5% forever, with R = 12%. Because g1 = 30% is above R, the analyst says the two-stage formula cannot be used. What is the right response?
options: She is right: the model fails whenever any growth rate in the forecast is above the required return R
The formula still works: only g2 must be below R, and the two negative factors multiply to a positive value
Replace g1 with R so that the denominator R − g1 is positive and the formula can then be used
Use the Gordon model with g = 30% for the whole stream, since the growth rate is above R
questions.explanation: Only the infinite stage needs g < R. For the first stage D1/(R − g1) and [1 − ((1 + g1)/(1 + R))^N] are both negative when g1 > R, and their product is positive (SM 8-23 uses g1 = 28% with R = 13%).

questions.stem: How does the two-stage formula relate to the timeline method (list every dividend, add the discounted horizon price)?
options: The formula is an approximation that is usually a few dollars too high
The timeline method values only the dividends, the formula also adds the horizon price
They give the same value; the formula bundles the first N discounted dividends into one growing-annuity term
They differ because the formula discounts at g1 while the timeline discounts at R
questions.explanation: Both methods discount the same cash flows at R: N growing dividends and the horizon price P_N. The growing-annuity term simply sums the discounted dividends in one step, which is quicker for long first stages (8 or 11 years in SM 8-23 and 8-24).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an input to the two-stage dividend formula?
options: The number of years N of first-stage growth
The long-run growth rate g2
The market price P0, which is the output of the model
The current dividend D0 (or D1)
questions.explanation: The formula needs D0 (or D1), g1, N, g2 and R, and produces the value P0. The market price is what you compare that value with afterwards; it is not an input.

questions.stem: Why does the two-stage formula need the second term P_N/(1 + R)^N in addition to the growing-annuity term?
options: The annuity term already contains all the dividends but ignores the time value of money
The second term converts the first-stage growth rate g1 into the long-run rate g2
The second term adjusts the first-stage dividends for the extra risk of fast growth
The annuity covers only N dividends; the tail from year N+1 on is worth P_N at date N and must be discounted back
questions.explanation: The growing-annuity formula covers exactly N dividends. The infinite tail after year N is valued by Gordon at date N (P_N), and a date-N value is brought to date 0 with (1 + R)^N.

questions.stem: True or false: in the two-stage model with D0 just paid, the horizon price is P_N = D0(1 + g1)^N(1 + g2)/(R − g2).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. D_N = D0(1 + g1)^N, and the first long-run dividend is D_{N+1} = D_N(1 + g2). The Gordon formula then values it at date N with R − g2 in the denominator.

questions.stem: In a two-stage valuation with g1 = 20% above g2 = 4% (R and D0 unchanged), what happens to P0 if the high-growth period N is lengthened from 5 to 8 years?
options: P0 falls, because the horizon price is discounted over three more years and g1 is above R
P0 is unchanged, because the horizon price depends only on g2 and R, not on N
P0 rises: there are more years of 20% growth, and the long-run phase starts from a larger dividend
P0 rises, but only through the growing-annuity term; the horizon term is unaffected
questions.explanation: A longer first stage means D_{N+1} is much larger and the 20% growth lasts longer; the extra discounting is outweighed by the extra growth (when g1 > g2). The change shows up in both terms, not only in the annuity term.

questions.stem: A two-stage valuation using your inputs gives $48.00 per share, while the stock trades at $55.00. What is the most direct reading?
options: The stock is undervalued at your inputs, so you should buy it at the $55.00 price
The model is invalid, because a correct DCF value must always equal the market price
The market price must be wrong, because a DCF value is always the true price of the stock
At your inputs the stock looks overvalued: the market assumes more growth or a lower R than you do
questions.explanation: A DCF value below the quote means that the price embeds more optimistic growth or a lower discount rate than your inputs. It does not prove the market wrong, but at your assumptions you would not pay $55.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards just paid a dividend of $2.20. Dividends will grow 22% per year for 4 years and 5% per year thereafter. R = 12% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: Annuity term = 2.684/(0.12 − 0.22) × [1 − (1.22/1.12)^4] = $10.9476. D5 = 2.20 × 1.22^4 × 1.05 = $5.1174, P4 = D5/0.07 = $73.1060, PV = $46.4602. P0 = $57.41. Using D4 in the horizon numerator gives $55.20; leaving P4 undiscounted gives $84.05; dropping the annuity term gives only $46.46.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Foods just paid $1.80. Dividends will grow 9% per year for 6 years and 3% per year forever after that. R = 11% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: Annuity term = D1/(R − g1)[1 − (1.09/1.11)^6] with D1 = 1.962: $10.1390. D7 = 1.80 × 1.09^6 × 1.03 = $3.1093; P6 = D7/(0.11 − 0.03) = $38.8668; PV = $20.7798. P0 = $30.92. Starting the annuity from D0 gives $30.08; running the annuity formula with g2 gives $29.65; discounting P6 seven years gives $28.86.

questions.stem: Tundra Telecom just paid $0.95. Dividends will grow 35% per year for 3 years and 6% per year forever after that. R = 13% per annum. What is the price today?
questions.explanation: With g1 = 35% > R both R − g1 = −0.22 and the bracket are negative: annuity term = +$4.1108. D4 = 0.95 × 1.35³ × 1.06 = $2.4776; P3 = D4/0.07 = $35.3943; PV = $24.5300. P0 = $28.64. Flipping the sign of the annuity term gives $20.42; using g2 in the annuity gives $27.73; putting D3 in the horizon numerator gives $27.25.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards just paid a dividend of $1.15. Dividends will grow 26% per year for the next 6 years and 4.5% per year thereafter, forever. R = 12% per annum. Use the two-stage formula to find the price today. (Answer in $.)

steps.label: First long-run dividend D7 = D0(1 + g1)^6(1 + g2)

errors.label: Used D6 instead of D7 in the horizon price
errors.explain: The horizon price needs the first long-run dividend D_{N+1} = D6 × 1.045, not D6.

errors.label: Added P6 without discounting it
errors.explain: P6 is a year-6 value; divide by (1 + R)^6 before adding it to a present-value term.

errors.label: Started the annuity from D0 instead of D1
errors.explain: The growing-annuity formula takes the NEXT dividend D1 = D0(1 + g1).

questions.explanation: A two-stage value is a growing annuity for the high-growth years plus the discounted horizon price. With g1 above R the annuity pieces are negative but their product is positive. The horizon price supplies about three quarters of the value.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Foods just paid $1.80 per share. Dividends are expected to grow 9% per year for 6 years and then 3% per year forever. R = 11% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Used g2 in the growing-annuity term
errors.explain: The first-stage dividends grow at g1; g2 belongs only in the horizon price.

errors.label: Started the annuity from D0
errors.explain: The annuity formula needs D1 = D0(1 + g1) = 1.962.

errors.label: Discounted P6 for seven years
errors.explain: P6 is a year-6 value, so it is discounted six periods.

questions.explanation: When g1 < R the pieces are all positive and the first stage contributes about a third of the value. The two methods (timeline or formula) must agree; the formula is just quicker.

questions.stem: Foothills Robotics just paid $0.85. Dividends will grow 21% per year for 9 years and then 4% per year forever. R = 11% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Used D9 in the horizon numerator
errors.explain: P9 values the dividends from D10 on; the numerator must be D10 = D9(1.04).

errors.label: Added P9 undiscounted
errors.explain: Discount P9 nine periods before adding it.

errors.label: Used only 8 years in the annuity term
errors.explain: The exponent N counts the dividends in the high-growth stage (9 here), and must match the discounting of P9.

questions.explanation: Nine years at 21% grow the dividend more than fivefold, so by year 9 the long-run dividend is large. The horizon piece is again the larger share of value, but the long first stage adds about $12.

questions.stem: Chinook Chemicals just paid $0.60. Dividends will grow 32% per year for 5 years and 6% per year forever after that. R = 12% per annum. What is the price today? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Flipped the sign of the annuity term
errors.explain: A negative R − g1 times a negative bracket is positive: the first-stage dividends add value.

errors.label: Used g1 in the horizon price (P5 = D6/(R − g1))
errors.explain: The long-run rate g2 = 6% belongs in the horizon price; g1 = 32% exceeds R and gives a negative price.

errors.label: Used 4 years in the annuity bracket but discounted P5 five years
errors.explain: The number of high-growth dividends N must be the same in the bracket and in the horizon date.

questions.explanation: Even with g1 far above R, the first-stage dividends are finite and add value (about $5). Only the infinite stage must have g2 < R.

questions.stem: Laurentian Labs just paid total dividends of $6.4 million. Total dividends will grow 24% per year for 4 years and 5% per year forever after that. R = 13% per annum and there are 10 million shares. What is the value per share today? (Answer in $ per share.)
keystrokes: Work in $ millions, then divide by 10 million shares at the end
6.4 × 1.24 = 7.936; annuity as before; P4: 6.4 × 1.24 y^x 4 × 1.05 ÷ 0.08 = 198.6; discount four years

errors.label: Forgot to divide by shares (answered in $ millions)
errors.explain: The model values the whole equity; divide by the number of shares to get a price per share.

errors.label: Used D4 instead of D5 in the horizon numerator
errors.explain: The horizon value needs the first long-run dividend D5 = D4 × 1.05.

errors.label: Did not discount the horizon value
errors.explain: P4 is a year-4 amount: discount it four periods.

questions.explanation: The same two-stage machinery works on total dividends; convert to per-share only at the end (or divide D0 by shares at the start).

questions.stem: In non-constant growth, "solving backwards" means:
options: computing the horizon price first and then discounting it back to date 0 to get today's price
the price is given (P0 or a horizon price) and you solve the valuation equation for an unknown input such as g2 or a dividend
valuing the stock by working from the last dividend toward the first dividend
discounting the dividends at the required return in reverse order, last dividend first
questions.explanation: In the usual direction the inputs (dividends, growth, R) give a price. Solving backwards flips this: the price is known and one input (g2, D1 or D0, the first dividend) is the unknown. The valuation equation is the same; you rearrange it.

questions.stem: Which of the following questions requires solving backwards?
options: "What is the stock worth today if dividends grow at 7% for three years and 5% afterwards forever?"
"What is the dividend yield if the stock trades at $20 and the next dividend D1 is $1.10 per share?"
"The stock should sell for $20 in three years. What growth rate after year 3 does that imply?"
"By how many periods is the horizon price discounted to bring it back to date 0?"
questions.explanation: Only the prompt that starts from the expected $20 price in three years and asks for the growth rate that price implies solves backwards: the price is known and an input (g2) is the unknown. The others run forward from inputs to a value or a ratio. Giant's "expected constant growth rate beginning in year 4" is the model case (S4 s9-13).

questions.stem: The horizon price P_T = D_T(1 + g2)/(R − g2) is known, together with D_T and R. Which expression gives g2?
options: g2 = (P_T × R − D_T)/(P_T − D_T)
g2 = R − D_T/P_T
g2 = (P_T × R + D_T)/(P_T + D_T)
g2 = (P_T × R − D_T)/(P_T + D_T)
questions.explanation: P_T(R − g2) = D_T(1 + g2) → P_T R − D_T = g2 (P_T + D_T). The shortcut R − D_T/P_T forgets that the next dividend is D_T(1 + g2), not D_T, so it overstates g2; the other two slip a sign when collecting the g2 terms.

questions.stem: The price today and all growth rates are known, but the current dividend D0 is not. The cleanest way to find D0 is to:
options: guess D0 and keep adjusting the required return until the price matches
find the horizon price and divide it by the number of years to the first dividend
write every discounted cash flow as a multiple of D0, add the multiples, and divide P0 by that total
average the growth rates and apply the Gordon formula backwards to D1
questions.explanation: With R and the growth rates fixed, every term of the valuation is D0 times a known factor, so P0 = D0 × (sum of factors) and D0 = P0/(sum). SM 8-18 gets a factor of 53.75 and D0 = $76/53.75 = $1.41.

questions.stem: Compare solving a non-constant growth model for D0 with solving it for the required return R. Which statement is correct?
options: D0 appears linearly, so algebra is enough; R is in every denominator, so it needs trial and error
Both can be rearranged to a closed form in one step, since each appears once in the equation
R has a closed form, but D0 needs trial and error because it multiplies every term
Neither can be solved, because the horizon price itself depends on the unknown quantity
questions.explanation: P0 = D0 × (known factors) is linear in D0. But R is inside (1 + R)^t and also inside R − g2 of the horizon price, so SM 8-33 finds R = 13.43% by root-finding. (Constant growth alone gives R = D1/P0 + g, which is closed form.)

questions.stem: Which of the following can NOT be found by simple algebra from a non-constant growth valuation?
options: The long-run growth rate g2 implied by a given horizon price
The dividend D0 implied by today's price and the growth rates
The required return R implied by the price (needs trial and error)
The horizon price that would give a chosen target value today
questions.explanation: g2, D0 and the needed horizon price each appear linearly (or in a simple ratio) once the others are known. R sits in several powers of (1 + R) and in R − g2, so SM 8-33 uses a root-finder to get 13.43%.

questions.stem: Why is D0 easy to solve for from today's price, even when growth rates change several times?
options: The horizon price does not depend on D0, so only the early dividends matter
Every dividend is D0 times known growth factors, so the valuation is P0 = D0 × (a known number)
Dividends cancel out of the present-value equation when growth rates change
The required return can be set equal to the growth rate, which removes D0 from the equation
questions.explanation: Each dividend is D0(1 + g1)(1 + g2)... and each discount factor is known, so the equation has a single unknown with a constant coefficient. That coefficient (e.g. 53.75 in SM 8-18) is the PV of the stream per $1 of D0.

questions.stem: An analyst's target price of $20 in three years implies a long-run dividend growth rate g2 = 9.8% when R = 11%. How should you read this?
options: The target is conservative, because g2 is comfortably less than R
The target is very optimistic: g2 is close to R, far above plausible long-run growth
The target is irrelevant, because g2 does not affect the horizon price
The implied g2 means the stock must be undervalued today, so buy it
questions.explanation: A horizon price P_T = D_{T+1}/(R − g2) becomes extremely sensitive when g2 approaches R. An implied g2 near R signals that the target needs near-perpetual high growth. Compare with Giant (S4 s11), where g2 = 5.32% against R = 15%.

questions.stem: Gatineau Glass just paid $1.20. Dividends grow 9% per year for 3 years, and the stock is expected to be worth $24.00 at the end of year 3 (R = 14% per annum). What constant growth rate g2 after year 3 does that price imply?
questions.explanation: D3 = 1.20 × 1.09³ = $1.5540. From 24 = D3(1 + g2)/(0.14 − g2): g2 = (24 × 0.14 − 1.5540)/(24 + 1.5540) = 7.0672%. The shortcut R − D3/P3 (7.52%) treats D3 as next year's dividend; using D0 gives 8.57%; (P − D) in the denominator gives 8.05%.

questions.stem: Harbourfront Bakeries trades at $60 today. Its dividend will grow 20% next year, 10% the year after, and 4% per year from year 3 on. R = 9% per annum. What is next year's dividend D1?
questions.explanation: Per $1 of D0: PV = 1.2/1.09 + 1.32/1.09² + (1.32 × 1.04/0.05)/1.09² = 25.3211. D0 = 60/25.3211 = $2.3696, so D1 = 1.20 × D0 = $2.84. Reporting D0 ($2.37) answers the wrong question; dropping the horizon price gives $32.55; discounting the horizon price three years gives $3.08.

questions.stem: Whitecap Wind just paid $2.40. Dividends grow 8% per year for 3 years. Analysts expect the stock to be worth $48.00 at the end of year 3, and R = 13% per annum. What constant growth rate g2 after year 3 is implied? (Answer in % per annum.)

steps.label: Implied long-run growth g2 = (P3 R − D3)/(P3 + D3) (in %)

errors.label: Treated D3 as the next dividend (g2 = R − D3/P3)
errors.explain: The horizon price uses D4 = D3(1 + g2), which still contains the unknown g2.

errors.label: Used D0 instead of D3
errors.explain: The dividend that grows into the long-run stream is D3, the last first-stage dividend.

errors.label: Collected the g2 terms with a sign slip

questions.explanation: With the horizon price given, the Gordon formula P3 = D3(1 + g2)/(R − g2) is one equation in one unknown. g2 = 6.30% is sensible against R = 13%.

questions.stem: Rideau Rail trades at $52.00. Its dividend is expected to grow 25% next year, 15% the year after, and 5% per year from year 3 on. R = 10% per annum. What is the dividend D1 due next year? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: Horizon price per $1 of D0: P2/D0 = 1.25 × 1.15 × 1.05/(R − g)
PV of everything per $1 of D0

solution: Write each cash flow per $1 of D0: D1 = 1.25, D2 = 1.4375, D3 = 1.5094

errors.label: Reported D0 instead of D1
errors.explain: The question asks for next year's dividend D1 = 1.25 D0.

errors.label: Left the horizon price out of the factor
errors.explain: The constant-growth tail after year 2 is by far the largest part of the factor.

errors.label: Discounted the horizon price three years
errors.explain: D3 is the first constant-growth dividend, so P2 is a year-2 value and is discounted twice.

questions.explanation: A solve-for-the-dividend problem is a forward valuation per $1 of D0 followed by a division. The horizon price carries most of the factor.

questions.stem: Yukon Drillers is expected to pay $1.10, $1.30, $1.55 and $1.80 at the ends of years 1 to 4. R = 11% per annum. What price would the stock have to reach at the end of year 4 for a buyer today to be willing to pay $55.00? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: PV that the year-4 price must supply

solution: The year-4 price must supply 55.00 − 4.3652 = $50.6348 in present value

errors.label: Ignored the dividends (P4 = 55 × 1.11^4)
errors.explain: The four dividends already pay back about $4.37 of the price, so P4 only has to cover the remainder.

errors.label: Compounded the remainder only three years
errors.explain: P4 is a year-4 value: compound the needed present value four periods.

errors.label: Added the dividends instead of subtracting
errors.explain: The dividends reduce, not increase, what the final price must be worth.

questions.explanation: Solving backwards for a horizon price is the same equation as the forward valuation: P0 = PV(dividends) + P4/(1 + R)^4, rearranged for P4.

questions.stem: Saskatoon Seed Corp trades at $18.40. It will pay no dividend for five years; its first dividend D6 arrives at the end of year 6 and then grows 6% per year forever. R = 12% per annum. What first dividend D6 is the market price implying? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Compounded six years instead of five
errors.explain: P5 (not P6) is one period before the first dividend, so compound P0 five periods.

errors.label: Used R + g
errors.explain: The Gordon denominator is R minus g.

errors.label: Skipped the compounding (D6 = P0 × (R − g))
errors.explain: Today's price is a present value; the dividend is paid years later, so you must compound P0 forward to year 5 first.

questions.explanation: Rearranging P0 = [D6/(R − g)]/(1 + R)^5 gives D6 = P0 × (1 + R)^5 × (R − g). The market is pricing in a first dividend of about $1.95.

questions.stem: The plowback ratio b is:
options: the fraction of earnings paid out as dividends, DPS/EPS
the fraction of earnings retained and reinvested, b = (EPS − DPS)/EPS
the growth rate of book equity per share
earnings per share divided by book equity per share
questions.explanation: Plowback (retention) is what the firm keeps: b = (EPS − DPS)/EPS = 1 − payout. The payout ratio DPS/EPS is its complement, and EPS divided by book equity per share is ROE.

questions.stem: In g = b × ROE as used in this course, ROE is earnings per share divided by:
options: book equity per share at the END of the year
the average of start-of-year and end-of-year book equity
book equity per share at the START of the year
the current market price per share
questions.explanation: Retained earnings added during the year raise equity at the end of the year, so the start-of-year base is the equity that earned this year's EPS. Dividing by end-of-year equity (or market price) understates ROE and therefore g.

questions.stem: A firm earns EPS of $3.00 and pays DPS of $1.20. Which pair of ratios describes it?
options: Plowback 60%, payout 40%
Plowback 40%, payout 60%
Plowback 60%, payout 60%
Plowback 40%, payout 40%
questions.explanation: Payout = 1.20/3.00 = 40%. Plowback is the rest: b = (3.00 − 1.20)/3.00 = 60%. The two always add to 100%; swapping them is the payout-as-plowback slip that produces g = payout × ROE.

questions.stem: A mature firm with ROE = 12% raises its payout ratio from 40% to 70% and ROE does not change. Its growth rate g changes from:
questions.explanation: g = b × ROE with b = 1 − payout: 0.60 × 12% = 7.2% before, and 0.30 × 12% = 3.6% after. Paying out more retains less, so growth falls. The other pairs use the payout ratio as if it were b.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes the payout ratio from the plowback ratio correctly?
options: Payout drives growth through g = payout × ROE; plowback is paid to shareholders
Payout = DPS/EPS goes to shareholders now; plowback b = 1 − payout drives growth through g = b × ROE
Payout and plowback are the same quantity measured on different dates
Plowback is measured on book equity, payout on the market price
questions.explanation: The cash paid out today is the payout; what stays in the firm to earn ROE next year is b. Only b enters g = b × ROE. Using the payout ratio there is the single most common slip on this topic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the course's growth relationship g = b × ROE?
options: A firm that retains all earnings and earns ROE of 14% grows at 14%
A firm that pays out all earnings still grows at ROE
At a constant ROE, raising the payout ratio lowers g
Growth comes from reinvested earnings that earn ROE on equity
questions.explanation: If b = 0 (everything paid out) then g = 0 × ROE = 0: no new equity is added, so book equity and earnings stay flat. The other statements follow directly from g = b × ROE.

questions.stem: Why do young companies typically plow back more than mature companies?
options: Young firms earn lower ROE, so they must reinvest more just to be able to pay dividends
Plowback is required by law for firms under five years old with no earnings history
Young firms have lower required returns, so they can afford to pay no dividends at all
They have many projects worth funding and need the cash, so b is near 1 and g is large
questions.explanation: Growth stocks reinvest nearly all earnings (b near 1, large g) because their opportunities are plentiful; income stocks have b near 0 and small g (L04 s29). Reinvestment is a response to opportunities, not a legal rule.
questions.ref: L04 s29; REV p3; SM 8 CTQ 3

questions.stem: A firm with R = 12% considers raising b. When will a higher plowback ratio increase the share price, holding R fixed?
options: Always, because a higher b raises g
When ROE is below R, because retained earnings are then cheaper than new equity
Never, because dividends are the only source of value
When ROE exceeds R: the reinvested earnings then earn more than investors require
questions.explanation: A higher b lowers D1 but raises g. If ROE > R each retained dollar is worth more than a dollar to shareholders (NPVGO rises); if ROE < R the growth destroys value, as in Johnson (S4 s18). If ROE = R, b makes no difference to price.

questions.stem: A firm with a return on equity of 15% and a payout ratio of 40% would expect a growth rate of:
options: None of the above
questions.explanation: Plowback b = 1 − payout = 1 − 0.40 = 0.60, so g = b × ROE = 0.60 × 15% = 9%. The tempting 6% comes from multiplying the payout ratio by ROE (0.40 × 15%: payout-as-plowback). The 21% and 24% add 15% × payout or 15% × b onto ROE, which has no basis in g = b × ROE.

questions.stem: Tamarack Solar wants its dividends to grow 7.5% per year and earns ROE = 12.5% on start-of-year equity. What plowback ratio b does it need? (Answer as a percentage.)
questions.explanation: g = b × ROE → b = g/ROE = 7.5%/12.5% = 60%. Reporting the payout ratio (40%) answers the complement; multiplying g by ROE gives 0.94%; solving the textbook sustainable-growth formula ROE·b/(1 − ROE·b) for b gives 55.81%, which is not the course formula.

questions.stem: Rideau Rail earned $2.4 million after tax, paid $0.96 million in dividends, and had book equity of $16.0 million at the start of the year. What growth rate does the course's formula give?
questions.explanation: b = (2.4 − 0.96)/2.4 = 0.60 and ROE = 2.4/16.0 = 15% on start-of-year equity, so g = 0.60 × 15% = 9.00%. Using the payout ratio (0.40) gives 6.00%; dividing by end-of-year equity (16.0 + 1.44 = 17.44) gives ROE 13.76% and g = 8.26%; and reporting ROE itself (15.00%) forgets to multiply by b.

questions.stem: Sun Peaks Resorts just reported EPS of $3.50 and pays out 45% of earnings; ROE is 14% and R = 11.5% per annum. Assuming payout and ROE stay constant, what is the share price?
True or false: if a firm pays out all of its earnings as dividends, then g = b × ROE gives a growth rate of zero.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With full payout b = 0, so no earnings are retained, book equity does not grow and g = 0 × ROE = 0. This is the 'no-growth' case behind the value EPS1/R.

questions.stem: Cobalt Peak Software reported EPS of $4.20 and DPS of $1.68 for the year just ended; book equity per share at the start of the year was $28.00. Payout and ROE stay constant and R = 12% per annum. What is the share price today? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: ROE = EPS/book equity at start of year

errors.label: Used the payout ratio as b (g = 6%)
errors.explain: Plowback is the retained share, 60%, not the 40% paid out.

errors.label: Measured ROE on end-of-year equity
errors.explain: ROE uses start-of-year equity (28.00); end-of-year equity includes the earnings just retained.

errors.label: Used DPS instead of D1
errors.explain: The Gordon numerator is next year's dividend D1 = DPS(1 + g).

questions.explanation: Steps: plowback → ROE on start-of-year equity → g = b × ROE → D1 = DPS(1 + g) → Gordon. The trailing P/E is about 14.5, sensible for g = 9% and R = 12%.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards earned net income of $14.7 million, paid dividends of $5.3 million, and had book equity of $98.0 million at the start of the year. Payout and ROE stay constant. What growth rate does the course's formula imply? (Answer in % per annum.)

errors.label: Used the payout ratio as b
errors.explain: b is what is retained (about 64%), not what is paid out.

errors.label: Used end-of-year equity (98 + 14.7 − 5.3)
errors.explain: ROE is measured on start-of-year equity.

errors.label: Reported ROE itself as the growth rate
errors.explain: g = b × ROE; skipping b treats every dollar of earnings as retained.

questions.explanation: Net income and dividends give b, net income and starting equity give ROE; their product is the growth rate (about 9.6%). The same answer comes from EPS and DPS per share.

questions.stem: Gatineau Glass just reported EPS of $5.00. It pays out 35% of earnings, ROE is 14% on start-of-year equity, and R = 13% per annum. Payout and ROE stay constant. What is the share price today? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: Next dividend D1 = EPS0 × payout × (1 + g)

errors.label: Used EPS0 × payout as D1 (no growth step)
errors.explain: D1 = payout × EPS1 and EPS1 = EPS0(1 + g); EPS0 is last year's number.

errors.label: Grew the dividend twice
errors.explain: Only one growth step separates D0 from D1.

questions.explanation: EPS0 is already earned; the dividend investors receive next year is payout × EPS1, where EPS1 = EPS0(1 + g).

questions.stem: Bow Valley Utilities reported EPS of $2.50 and DPS of $1.00. ROE is 12% on start-of-year equity, payout and ROE stay constant, and R = 10.5% per annum. What do you expect the share price to be three years from now? (Answer in $.)

steps.label: Price today P0 = DPS(1 + g)/(R − g)
Price in three years P3 = P0(1 + g)^3

solution: With constant growth the price grows at g: P3 = 32.4848 × 1.072³ = $40.02

errors.label: Stopped at today's price
errors.explain: The question asks for the price three years ahead; it has grown at g.

errors.label: Used D0 = 1.00 in the Gordon numerator
Grew the price at R (10.5%) instead of g
errors.explain: Under constant growth the price rises at g, not R (R is the total return including dividends).

questions.explanation: Constant growth means price, dividend and earnings all grow at g = b × ROE. The 7.2% growth rate is what carries today's $32.48 to $40.02.

questions.stem: Peace River Foods wants dividends to grow 8% per year while paying out 55% of earnings. What ROE (on start-of-year equity) does it need? (Answer in % per annum.)

errors.label: Divided g by the payout ratio
errors.explain: g = b × ROE with b = 0.45, so ROE = 0.08/0.45.

errors.label: Multiplied g by b
errors.explain: To isolate ROE, divide g by b; multiplying gives a growth-like number.

questions.explanation: Rearranging g = b × ROE gives ROE = g/b. A high payout leaves little to reinvest, so each retained dollar must earn a lot (17.8%).

questions.stem: The forward P/E ratio is:
options: the price divided by the earnings of the year just ended, P0/EPS0, which is the trailing ratio
forecast earnings divided by the current price, EPS1/P0, which is the earnings yield
the price expected next year divided by this year's earnings, P1/EPS0 under constant growth
the price divided by forecast earnings for the coming year, P0/EPS1 = (1 − b)/(R − g) under constant growth
questions.explanation: Forward P/E uses next year's earnings in the denominator; with D1 = (1 − b)EPS1 and P0 = D1/(R − g) it simplifies to (1 − b)/(R − g). Using last year's earnings gives the trailing P/E, and E/P is the earnings yield.

questions.stem: A stock trades at $42. Analysts expect earnings of $3.00 per share over the next twelve months, and the company earned $2.80 over the last twelve months. Which ratio equals 42/3.00 = 14.0?
options: The forward P/E
The trailing P/E
The earnings yield
The dividend yield
questions.explanation: Price over forecast earnings is the forward P/E (42/3.00 = 14.0). The trailing P/E would use the $2.80 already earned (15.0), and the earnings yield is the inverse, E/P.

questions.stem: For a company whose earnings are expected to grow, how do the trailing and forward P/E ratios compare?
options: The forward P/E is higher, because the future is more uncertain than the past
They are equal, because both ratios use exactly the same current price
The forward P/E is lower only if the firm pays no dividend at all
The forward P/E is lower: the same price is divided by larger forecast earnings
questions.explanation: Trailing = P0/EPS0 and forward = P0/EPS1. With EPS1 > EPS0 and the same P0, forward < trailing; their ratio is 1 + g. If earnings are expected to fall the order reverses.

questions.stem: Two firms have the same R and the same growth rate g. Firm X pays out 60% of earnings and Firm Y pays out 30%. Which has the higher forward P/E and why?
options: Firm X: (1 − b) is larger, so more of each dollar of EPS1 is paid as dividends at the same g
Firm Y: it retains more, so each dollar of its earnings is worth more to shareholders
They have the same P/E, because R and g are the same for both firms
Firm Y: retaining more always raises growth, so it must be worth more per dollar
questions.explanation: Forward P/E = (1 − b)/(R − g). With R and g equal, a higher payout (lower b) raises the numerator. Equal g with lower b means X's ROE is higher; X delivers the same growth while paying out more. (Raising b with ROE fixed would raise g, but here g is held equal.)

questions.stem: Why does a higher required return R lower the forward P/E?
options: A higher R raises the growth rate g by the same amount, so the two cancel out in the ratio
A higher R lowers the forecast EPS1 that sits in the denominator of the P/E ratio
A higher R lowers the payout ratio, so the numerator (1 − b) falls as well
R − g rises, so each dollar of next year's dividend is worth fewer dollars of price
questions.explanation: P/E = (1 − b)/(R − g): R only appears in the denominator. A riskier stock (higher R) is discounted more heavily, so the same earnings and growth buy a lower multiple (L04 s31, point 2).

questions.stem: Other things equal, which of the following would NOT raise a firm's forward P/E?
options: A higher expected growth rate g in dividends
A higher required return R for a riskier firm
A lower required return R for the stock
A higher payout ratio with growth g unchanged
questions.explanation: The three professor's rules: high g, low R and high payout (with g constant) all raise (1 − b)/(R − g). A riskier stock has a higher R, which lowers the multiple.

questions.stem: A stock has a forward P/E of 9 while similar firms trade near 15. Which interpretation is consistent with P/E = (1 − b)/(R − g)?
options: The firm must have a higher payout ratio than its peers
The firm's earnings are overstated, so the multiple is mechanically too low
The market expects lower growth or requires a higher return for this firm (or it is mispriced)
The firm must have higher growth, since low P/E signals growth
questions.explanation: A low multiple means a small (1 − b)/(R − g): either R − g is large (low g or high R) or the firm is simply undervalued relative to comparables. Low P/E is the signature of an income or risky stock, not a growth stock.

questions.stem: True or false: under constant growth the forward P/E equals (1 − b)/(R − g).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. P0 = D1/(R − g) and D1 = (1 − b)EPS1, so P0/EPS1 = (1 − b)/(R − g).

questions.stem: Kodiak Fibre retains 35% of earnings, earns ROE = 16%, and investors require R = 11% per annum. What is its forward P/E?
questions.explanation: g = b × ROE = 0.35 × 16% = 5.6%, so P/E = (1 − 0.35)/(0.11 − 0.056) = 0.65/0.054 = 12.04. The 1/(R − g) shortcut (18.52) forgets the dividend share (1 − b); treating 0.35 as the payout flips b and gives 58.33; ignoring g gives 5.91.

questions.stem: Trillium Trucking pays out 60% of earnings, expects dividend growth of 6% per year, and R = 10% per annum. What is its forward P/E?
questions.explanation: Forward P/E = (1 − b)/(R − g) = payout/(R − g) = 0.60/0.04 = 15.00. Using b = 40% in the numerator gives 10.00; adding g to R gives 3.75; dropping the payout gives 25.00.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards pays out 45% of earnings, earns ROE = 14% on start-of-year equity, and R = 11.5% per annum. Assuming constant payout and ROE, what is its forward P/E? (Answer as a multiple, 2 decimals.)

errors.label: Treated 45% as b
errors.explain: Payout is 45%, so b = 55%: g = 7.7% and the numerator is the payout 0.45.

errors.label: Dropped (1 − b)
errors.explain: P/E = P0/EPS1 and P0 only capitalises the dividend share (1 − b) of EPS1.

errors.label: Ignored growth in the denominator
errors.explain: R − g, not R, is the capitalisation rate.

questions.explanation: A 45% payout and 7.7% growth against R = 11.5% give a forward multiple near 12. Because the denominator is small, the multiple is very sensitive to g and R.

questions.stem: Prairie Grain Co-op just reported EPS of $3.85. It pays out 60% of earnings, ROE is 15%, R = 10.5% per annum, and payout and ROE stay constant. Use its forward P/E to find the share price today. (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Applied the forward P/E to EPS0
errors.explain: A forward multiple pairs with EPS1 = EPS0(1 + g), not with last year's EPS.

errors.label: Used the payout ratio as b (g = 9%)
errors.explain: Payout is 60%, so b = 40% and g = 6%.

errors.label: Grew EPS twice
errors.explain: One growth step from EPS0 gives EPS1.

questions.explanation: Forward P/E × EPS1 is the Gordon price. Mixing a forward multiple with trailing EPS understates the price by exactly the factor (1 + g).

questions.stem: Laurentian Labs has a forward P/E of 16.5, pays out 60% of earnings, and its dividends are expected to grow 5.5% per year. What required return R does the market price imply? (Answer in % per annum.)

errors.label: Forgot to add g back
errors.explain: R − g = 3.64% is the dividend yield D1/P0; the required return is yield plus g.

errors.label: Used b = 40% in the numerator
errors.explain: The numerator is the payout (1 − b) = 60%.

errors.label: Used the earnings yield 1/PE
errors.explain: 1/PE capitalises all earnings; only the payout share becomes dividends.

questions.explanation: Solving the forward P/E equation for R is the 'R = D1/P0 + g' relation in disguise: D1/P0 = (1 − b)/PE.

questions.stem: Rideau Rail has a forward P/E of 14.2 and its earnings are expected to grow 6.5% this year. What is its trailing P/E? (Answer as a multiple, 2 decimals.)
solution: Trailing = P0/EPS0 and forward = P0/EPS1, so trailing/forward = EPS1/EPS0 = 1 + g

errors.label: Divided by (1 + g)
errors.explain: Dividing gives a number smaller than the forward P/E; the trailing ratio must be the larger one for a growing firm.

errors.label: Subtracted growth instead of compounding
errors.explain: The link between the two is multiplicative: EPS1 = EPS0(1 + g).

questions.explanation: Same price, smaller denominator: trailing P/E exceeds forward P/E by the growth factor.

questions.stem: NPVGO stands for the net present value of growth opportunities. It is:
options: the net present value of the firm's single largest investment project
the present value of all future dividends, P0 = D1/(R − g)
the price the firm would have if it grew at the industry growth rate
the part of the price above the no-growth value: NPVGO = P0 − EPS1/R
questions.explanation: A firm with no growth has value EPS1/R (a perpetuity of its earnings). Whatever the market pays above that is the value of the growth opportunities: NPVGO = P0 − EPS1/R, so P0 = EPS1/R + NPVGO.

questions.stem: Which statement of the NPVGO relationship matches the formula sheet?
options: P0 = EPS0/R + NPVGO
P0 = EPS1/R + NPVGO
P0 = EPS1 × R + NPVGO
P0 = EPS1/(R − g) − NPVGO
questions.explanation: The no-growth value is next year's earnings capitalised at R. EPS0 is last year's number (eps0-for-eps1 error), multiplying by R inverts the perpetuity, and NPVGO is added to, not subtracted from, the no-growth value.

questions.stem: Fundy Marine expects EPS1 = $5.10 and R = 9% per annum. What does 5.10/0.09 = $56.67 represent?
options: The value of the firm's growth opportunities, NPVGO, per share
The value of the share if the firm paid out all earnings and never grew
The Gordon growth price of the share, P0 = D1/(R − g)
The share's book value per share taken from the balance sheet
questions.explanation: EPS1/R is a perpetuity of constant earnings: the no-growth value. NPVGO is the market price minus this number.

questions.stem: Your valuation shows that a stock's NPVGO is negative at your discount rate. Which conclusion matches the course?
options: The stock must be overvalued, so it should be sold if held or avoided at this price
NPVGO can never be negative, so there must be an arithmetic mistake in the valuation
Either undervalued (buy) or growth is destroying value (do not buy); the sign alone does not say
The firm should raise its plowback ratio to repair the negative NPVGO
questions.explanation: Professor Godfrey: NPVGO ought to be positive; if it is negative either the company is undervalued (you should buy it) or its growth opportunities destroy value (you should not). You must look at why the price is below EPS1/R.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates a firm's growth rate to its NPVGO?
options: Fast growth does not guarantee a positive NPVGO; growth adds value only if reinvestment earns more than R
Any positive growth rate produces a positive NPVGO, since earnings keep rising
NPVGO is positive exactly when the firm pays dividends to its shareholders
NPVGO depends on the growth rate but not on the required return R
questions.explanation: NPVGO measures value created by reinvestment, so it depends on ROE versus R, not on growth alone. Johnson Company grows 1% yet has NPVGO = −$7.06 (S4 s18), while Harrison grows 8% after year 6 and has NPVGO = +$68.14.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the NPVGO approach?
options: It uses last year's earnings EPS0 to value the no-growth stream
It splits price into a no-growth value and a growth component
A negative NPVGO can mean growth is destroying value
The no-growth value is EPS1/R
questions.explanation: The first dividend of the no-growth perpetuity arrives next year, so the numerator is EPS1, the forecast. Using EPS0 shifts the perpetuity one period and is the standard error (eps0-for-eps1).

questions.stem: Why does the NPVGO formula use EPS1 rather than EPS0?
options: EPS1 is always smaller than EPS0, which keeps NPVGO positive in the formula
EPS0 already includes the growth opportunities, so it would double count them
The formula sheet uses EPS1 because dividends are paid on forecast earnings only
A perpetuity is valued one period before its first payment, and next year's earnings are the first payment
questions.explanation: EPS1/R is the PV today of earnings EPS1, EPS1, EPS1... received at dates 1, 2, 3, ... Using EPS0 would value a stream starting at date 0 and overstate the no-growth value by one year of earnings.

questions.stem: From NPVGO, P/E = 1/R + NPVGO/EPS1. A firm with R = 10% has a forward P/E of 9. What does this say?
options: The firm has strongly positive growth opportunities
NPVGO is zero because P/E is close to 1/R
The P/E is below 1/R = 10, so NPVGO is negative
The required return must be exactly 9%
questions.explanation: 1/R = 10 is the multiple of a no-growth firm. A P/E of 9 sits below it, so NPVGO/EPS1 = 9 − 10 = −1 and NPVGO is negative. Compare Johnson (P/E 9.12 < 10) with Harrison (37.26 > 10) in Seminar 4.

questions.stem: A firm retains most of its earnings but earns only 8% on them (ROE = 8%) while shareholders require R = 12%. What does the NPVGO framework say?
options: NPVGO is positive, because retained earnings raise the growth rate
NPVGO is zero, because any positive ROE adds value
NPVGO is negative: shareholders would be better off if the earnings were paid out
NPVGO cannot be assessed without knowing the payout ratio
questions.explanation: Each retained dollar earns 8% when investors could earn 12% elsewhere, so reinvestment destroys value and the price falls below EPS1/R. This is the logic of the Johnson example.

questions.stem: A firm trades at $82.40 with EPS1 = $5.20 and R = 10%. What does it tell you that EPS1/R = $52.00?
options: The firm is overvalued by $52.00 relative to its earnings power
The firm's book equity is $52.00 per share on the balance sheet
The market expects the firm to pay a $52.00 dividend next year
About 37% of the price pays for growth opportunities; $52.00 is the no-growth value
questions.explanation: No-growth value $52.00 plus NPVGO $30.40 = price $82.40. Growth opportunities are 30.40/82.40 = 36.9% of the price.

questions.stem: Chinook Chemicals trades at $61.50. It earned $3.40 last year and analysts forecast EPS of $3.60 for next year. R = 9% per annum. What is NPVGO per share?
questions.explanation: NPVGO = P0 − EPS1/R = 61.50 − 3.60/0.09 = 61.50 − 40.00 = $21.50. Using last year's EPS ($3.40) gives $23.72; subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign (−$21.50); forgetting to divide by R gives $57.90.

questions.stem: A firm has R = 8%, EPS1 = $2.50 and NPVGO = $12.00 per share. Using P/E = 1/R + NPVGO/EPS1, what is its forward P/E?
questions.explanation: 1/R = 12.50 and NPVGO/EPS1 = 12.00/2.50 = 4.80, so P/E = 17.30. Adding the dollar NPVGO to 1/R (24.50) mixes dollars with a multiple; using only NPVGO/EPS1 (4.80) or only 1/R (12.50) leaves out one of the two pieces. Check: P0 = 17.30 × 2.50 = $43.25 = 31.25 + 12.00.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Brewing earned $2.00 this year and expects EPS1 = $2.10. R = 7% per annum and the value of its growth opportunities is NPVGO = $9.40 per share. What is the share price?
questions.explanation: No-growth value = EPS1/R = 2.10/0.07 = $30.00; adding NPVGO gives P0 = $39.40. Using this year's EPS gives $37.97; subtracting NPVGO gives $20.60; skipping the division by R gives $11.50.

questions.stem: Fundy Marine just paid a dividend of $3.80, which is expected to grow 2% per year forever. R = 9% per annum and next year's EPS is forecast at $5.10. What is its NPVGO per share? (Answer in $; a negative answer is possible.)
solution: Negative: either the shares are undervalued or growth destroys value (the firm retains a lot but grows only 2%).

errors.label: Used D0 in the Gordon numerator
Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: NPVGO is the market (model) price MINUS the no-growth value.

errors.label: Subtracted EPS1 without dividing by R
errors.explain: The no-growth value is the perpetuity EPS1/R.

questions.explanation: Fundy Marine pays out about 75% of EPS1 yet grows only 2%, so its retained earnings are earning little: growth destroys a little value (-$1.30). This is the Johnson pattern in Seminar 4.

questions.stem: Boreal Biotech pays no dividend for six years. Its first dividend, D7 = $4.20, comes at the end of year 7 and then grows 7% per year forever. R = 11.5% per annum and EPS1 is forecast at $1.95. What is NPVGO per share? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Discounted P6 seven years
errors.explain: P6 is a year-6 value (one period before D7).

errors.label: Did not discount P6 at all
errors.explain: P6 must be discounted to date 0 before comparing with EPS1/R.

errors.label: Grew D7 once more before dividing
errors.explain: D7 is already the first constant-growth dividend.

questions.explanation: More than two thirds of the price is growth value, typical of a young firm. NPVGO is positive, so growth creates value (Harrison pattern).

questions.stem: Whitecap Wind expects EPS1 = $6.00. It retains 60% of earnings, earns ROE = 10% on start-of-year equity, and R = 13% per annum. Payout and ROE stay constant. What is NPVGO per share? (Answer in $; the sign matters.)
solution: NPVGO = 34.2857 − 46.1538 = −$11.87: retaining at ROE 10% < R 13% destroys value

errors.label: Used 40% as b (g = 4%)
errors.explain: The firm retains 60%, so b = 0.60 and the dividend is 40% of EPS1.

errors.label: Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: NPVGO = P0 − EPS1/R, which is negative here.

errors.label: Compared P0 with EPS1 instead of EPS1/R
errors.explain: The no-growth value is the perpetuity EPS1/R = 46.15, not EPS1 itself.

questions.explanation: ROE (10%) is below R (13%), so each reinvested dollar is worth less than a dollar to shareholders: the more the firm retains, the lower NPVGO. Paying everything out would give $46.15.

questions.stem: Cobalt Peak Software trades at $82.40 with EPS1 = $5.20 forecast and R = 10% per annum. What percentage of its price is NPVGO? (Answer in %.)

errors.label: Gave the no-growth share of the price
errors.explain: That is the complement (63.1%); the question asks for the growth share.

errors.label: Divided NPVGO by the no-growth value instead of the price
errors.explain: The share of the PRICE uses P0 in the denominator; NPVGO/(EPS1/R) compares growth with the no-growth part (58.5%).

questions.explanation: Over a third of the price is growth value. The rest, $52, is what the current earnings alone are worth.

questions.stem: A stock trades at $64.00. You estimate its growth opportunities are worth NPVGO = $14.50 per share and R = 9.5% per annum. What EPS1 does that imply? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Added NPVGO instead of subtracting
errors.explain: NPVGO is part of the price, so the no-growth part is P0 − NPVGO.

errors.label: Stopped before multiplying by R
errors.explain: 49.50 is the no-growth value EPS1/R, not EPS1 itself.

questions.explanation: Rearranging P0 = EPS1/R + NPVGO gives EPS1 = (P0 − NPVGO) × R. It is the same relationship used backwards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about NPVGO?
options: NPVGO = EPS1/R − P0
NPVGO can never be negative
NPVGO uses this year's EPS0 in the no-growth value
NPVGO equals the market price of the stock
None of the above
questions.explanation: NPVGO = P0 − EPS1/R: the order is price minus the no-growth value (not the reverse), it can be negative (Johnson, S4 s18), the no-growth value uses next year's EPS1, and NPVGO is only the growth part of the price. None of the listed statements is correct.

questions.stem: From a quote screen, the earnings growth the market expects this year is implied by:
options: trailing P/E divided by forward P/E, minus 1
trailing P/E minus forward P/E
forward P/E divided by trailing P/E, minus 1
the dividend yield minus the forward dividend yield
questions.explanation: Trailing P/E = P0/EPS0 and forward P/E = P0/EPS1, so trailing ÷ forward = EPS1/EPS0 = 1 + g. Subtract 1 for the growth rate. The price cancels, so the market's expected growth is read off the two ratios.

questions.stem: A quote screen lists a price/earnings ratio of 21.37 and a consensus forward P/E of 19.52. Which question can be answered directly from these two numbers alone?
options: What is the company's required return R on its shares?
How many shares does the company have outstanding?
What EPS growth does the market expect this year?
What is the company's plowback ratio this year?
questions.explanation: The ratio 21.37/19.52 = EPS1/EPS0 gives expected EPS growth. Shares need the market capitalisation and price, R needs a dividend model, and plowback needs payout data.

questions.stem: A stock has trailing P/E of 18 and forward P/E of 16. Which expression gives the expected EPS growth?
questions.explanation: EPS1/EPS0 = (P0/16)/(P0/18) = 18/16, so g = 18/16 − 1 = 12.5%. Inverting the ratio gives −11.1%, the difference of the two multiples is not a growth rate, and dividing by the trailing multiple gives the wrong base (11.1%).

questions.stem: You know a stock's price, its trailing P/E and its forward P/E. To find next year's expected EPS you should:
options: divide the price by the forward P/E
divide the price by the trailing P/E
multiply the price by the forward P/E
multiply the trailing EPS by the forward P/E
questions.explanation: Forward P/E = P0/EPS1, so EPS1 = P0/forward P/E. Dividing by the trailing P/E gives EPS0, last year's earnings (a trailing-forward mix-up).

questions.stem: How does the growth implied by the trailing and forward P/E differ from the growth rate g in the Gordon model?
options: It is the same thing as Gordon's g, because both measure the market's expected growth
It measures dividend growth, whereas Gordon's g measures earnings growth
It is a long-run rate, whereas Gordon's g is a one-year growth rate
It is the expected EPS growth for one year; Gordon's g is a constant dividend growth rate forever
questions.explanation: A trailing/forward comparison only tells you EPS1/EPS0 for the next twelve months, which can be temporarily high or low. Gordon's g is a permanent rate used in P0 = D1/(R − g). They can be equal for a steady-growth firm but need not be.

questions.stem: Which of the following can NOT be found from a quote screen's price, market capitalisation, trailing P/E and forward P/E?
options: The number of shares outstanding
The company's required return R
Last year's EPS
Next year's expected net income
questions.explanation: Shares = market cap/price; EPS0 = price/trailing P/E; net income next year = price × shares/forward P/E. R is a property of investors' required compensation and needs a valuation model (R = D1/P0 + g), not just multiples.

questions.stem: Why is the forward P/E lower than the trailing P/E for a company whose earnings are expected to rise?
options: The price is the same, but the forward ratio divides it by a larger EPS
Forward earnings are discounted at a higher rate than trailing earnings
The price falls whenever earnings are forecast rather than reported as actual
Analysts deliberately forecast low earnings to make stocks look cheap
questions.explanation: P0 is the same in both ratios. EPS1 > EPS0 makes P0/EPS1 < P0/EPS0, and the gap between them is exactly the growth factor 1 + g.

questions.stem: A stock has trailing P/E 12.4 and forward P/E 13.6. What does the market expect for this year's earnings?
options: Growth of about 9.7%, because the forward P/E is higher than the trailing P/E
No change, because both P/E ratios use the same price
Growth of about 1.2%, which is the difference between the two ratios
A decline of about 8.8%, because forecast EPS is below last year's EPS
questions.explanation: 12.4/13.6 − 1 = −8.8%: the forward multiple is higher only because forecast EPS is lower than last year's. A forward P/E above the trailing P/E signals expected falling earnings.

questions.stem: A quote screen shows a trailing P/E of 22.4 and a consensus forward P/E of 20.0. What growth in EPS does the market expect this year?
questions.explanation: EPS1/EPS0 = 22.4/20.0 = 1.12, so g = 12.00%. The difference of the multiples (2.40) is not a growth rate; inverting the ratio gives -10.71%; leaving out the −1 gives 112%.

questions.stem: Harbourfront Bakeries trades at $36.00 and just paid a dividend of $1.44. If R = 10% per annum, what constant dividend growth rate does the price imply?
questions.explanation: 36 = 1.44(1 + g)/(0.10 − g) → 3.60 − 36g = 1.44 + 1.44g → g = (3.60 − 1.44)/(36 + 1.44) = 5.77%. The shortcut R − D0/P0 (6.00%) treats D0 as next year's dividend; adding D0 in the numerator gives 13.46%; adding the yield to R gives 14.00%.

questions.stem: A quote screen for Laurentian Labs shows a trailing price/earnings ratio of 21.37 and a consensus forward P/E of 19.52. What rate of growth in earnings per share is expected this year? (Answer in %.)
solution: Trailing P/E = P0/EPS0 and forward P/E = P0/EPS1

errors.label: Inverted the ratio (forward ÷ trailing − 1)
errors.explain: Forward EPS is the larger number, so the ratio that exceeds 1 is trailing ÷ forward.

errors.label: Subtracted the two multiples
errors.explain: The multiples are ratios of the same price; the growth factor is their quotient, not their difference.

errors.label: Forgot to subtract 1
errors.explain: 1.0948 is the growth factor 1 + g; g is the 0.0948.

questions.explanation: The price cancels out: trailing ÷ forward P/E = EPS1/EPS0. This is the calculation in part (b) of the sample-exam quote-screen question.

questions.stem: Rideau Rail trades at $45.60 with a trailing P/E of 15.2 and a forward P/E of 14.0. What EPS growth does the market expect this year? (Answer in %.)

errors.label: Reported EPS1/EPS0 as a percentage
errors.explain: The ratio 1.0857 includes the base; growth is the extra 8.57%.

errors.label: Divided the increase by EPS1 instead of EPS0
errors.explain: Growth is measured on the starting EPS0.

errors.label: Swapped trailing and forward
errors.explain: Trailing P/E is the larger one for a growing firm; the ratio forward ÷ trailing gives a decline.

questions.explanation: Going through EPS0 and EPS1 gives the same answer as the ratio shortcut and is a good check.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards trades at $48.00 and just paid a dividend of $1.92. If R = 9.5% per annum, what constant dividend growth rate does the market price imply? (Answer in % per annum.)

steps.label: Implied growth g = (P0 R − D0)/(P0 + D0) (in %)

errors.label: Used R − D0/P0
errors.explain: D0/P0 is not the dividend yield: the yield uses D1 = D0(1 + g).

errors.label: Added D0 to P0 R in the numerator
errors.explain: Collecting terms: P0 R − D0 = g (P0 + D0).

errors.label: Added the yield to R
errors.explain: R = yield + g, so g = R − yield, not R + yield.

questions.explanation: With D0 given, the algebra needs the (P0 + D0) denominator. If D1 were given, the shortcut g = R − D1/P0 would be exact.

questions.stem: Gatineau Glass trades at $38.40 with a market capitalisation of $2,400 million, a trailing P/E of 17.5 and a consensus forward P/E of 15.9. What net income does the market expect next year? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: Expected net income = EPS1 × shares ($ millions)

solution: Net income next year = 2.4151 × 62.5 = $150.94 million (also market cap ÷ forward P/E)

errors.label: Used the trailing P/E (this gives last year's income)
errors.explain: Dividing by the trailing P/E gives last year's net income, $137.14 million.

errors.label: Stopped at shares outstanding
errors.explain: 62.5 is the number of shares in millions; net income needs EPS1 as well.

questions.explanation: Net income = market cap ÷ P/E. With the forward ratio you get next year's expected income; with the trailing ratio, last year's. The ratio of the two is the implied growth (10.1% here).

questions.stem: Free cash flow to the firm (FCF or FCFF) is:
options: the cash left for shareholders after interest and debt repayments have been paid
net income after tax plus depreciation, before CAPEX and working capital
the after-tax cash from operations available to lenders and shareholders, EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
operating revenue minus operating expenses, which is EBITDA
questions.explanation: FCF is measured BEFORE any payment to capital providers, so it is built from EBIT, not from net income. The cash left for shareholders after lenders are paid is FCFE; EBITDA ignores tax, CAPEX and working capital.

questions.stem: Which expression is the free cash flow formula on the formula sheet?
options: NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
EBIT(1 − T) + D&A + CAPEX − ΔWC
EBIT(1 − T) − Interest + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
questions.explanation: FCF taxes EBIT as if the firm had no debt, adds back non-cash D&A, subtracts the cash spent on CAPEX and the cash tied up in working capital. NPAT-based and interest-based versions describe cash to shareholders, not to the whole firm; adding CAPEX has the wrong sign.

questions.stem: An analyst forecasts a firm's free cash flows and discounts them at the firm's overall discount rate. What does the result represent?
options: The value of the shareholders' equity after subtracting debt
The accounting book value of the firm's total assets
The present value of next year's dividend per share
Enterprise value (EV), the value of the operations to all investors
questions.explanation: FCF belongs to lenders and shareholders together, so its PV is EV. Equity is found afterwards: Equity = EV − Debt + Cash.

questions.stem: A firm's FCF has just been reported at $3.4 million and is expected to grow 3.5% per year forever. R = 9.5% per annum. Which expression gives EV?
questions.explanation: Constant growing FCF is a growing perpetuity: EV = FCF1/(R − g) with FCF1 = FCF0(1 + g). Using FCF0 is the d0-for-d1 error; dividing by R alone ignores growth; adding g to R is a sign slip.

questions.stem: How does FCF differ from net income (NPAT)?
options: FCF is after interest, whereas NPAT is calculated before any interest expense
FCF includes only operating revenue and expenses, whereas NPAT also includes tax
They are the same figure whenever the firm pays no dividend
FCF is before interest and deducts CAPEX and ΔWC; NPAT is after interest and ignores both
questions.explanation: NPAT is an accounting profit after interest and tax with depreciation deducted. FCF starts from EBIT(1 − T), so lenders' interest is not deducted, then converts profit to cash by adding back D&A and deducting reinvestment (CAPEX and ΔWC).

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT appear in the FCF formula?
options: The tax rate T applied to EBIT
Capital expenditures (CAPEX)
Interest expense and the change in debt
The change in working capital (ΔWC)
questions.explanation: Interest and ΔDebt are payments to and from lenders; FCF is the cash generated BEFORE those flows. They appear in FCFE (through NPAT and + ΔDebt), not in FCF.

questions.stem: Why is FCF built from EBIT(1 − T) rather than from net income?
options: Net income is not affected by taxes, so EBIT(1 − T) is the more accurate measure
EBIT is a cash figure while net income is a non-cash accounting figure
FCF is the cash for ALL capital providers, so it must not be reduced by interest paid to lenders
Interest is not a real expense for the firm, so it is always ignored in valuation
questions.explanation: Lenders and shareholders are both claimants on FCF. Deducting interest first would measure only what remains for shareholders (and also needs the matching ΔDebt, which is the FCFE route).

questions.stem: A fast-growing retailer reports negative FCF this year because CAPEX far exceeds D&A. What does this imply for its EV?
options: EV must be negative, because the first cash flow is negative and everything is discounted
EV equals zero until the year in which FCF first turns positive for the firm
The firm should be valued with the Gordon model using this year's FCF as D0
Nothing by itself: EV is the PV of ALL future FCFs, which may be large and positive later
questions.explanation: A growth firm reinvests heavily today and is valued on later cash flows (a non-constant growth timeline with horizon value). A negative first-year FCF cannot be run through FCF/R or FCF1/(R − g).

questions.stem: True or false: if FCFs are discounted to give enterprise value, the equity value is EV − Debt + Cash.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. EV = Equity + Debt − Cash, so Equity = EV − Debt + Cash. Cash is added back because it is not part of the operations valued by FCF but belongs to shareholders (net debt = Debt − Cash).

questions.stem: A software firm has EV = $80 million, debt of $5 million and cash of $25 million. Its equity value is:
options: $60 million, because debt and cash are both subtracted
$100 million, larger than EV because cash exceeds debt
$75 million, because debt is subtracted and cash ignored
$80 million, because equity equals EV
questions.explanation: Equity = EV − Debt + Cash = 80 − 5 + 25 = $100 million. With net cash (cash > debt), equity exceeds EV. Subtracting cash is the sign slip of confusing equity with EV.

questions.stem: Okanagan Brewing reports (in $ thousands): revenue 3,200; operating costs excluding D&A 2,150; D&A 250; interest 90. The tax rate is 30%, CAPEX is 300 and ΔWC is 40. What is its free cash flow?
options: $380 thousand
$407 thousand
$470 thousand
$550 thousand
questions.explanation: EBIT = 3,200 − 2,150 − 250 = 800; EBIT(1 − T) = 560. FCF = 560 + 250 − 300 − 40 = 470. Starting from NPAT (497) gives 407; subtracting interest from EBIT(1 − T) gives 380; adding ΔWC instead of subtracting gives 550.

questions.stem: A firm's free cash flows are worth an enterprise value of $120.0 million. It has debt of $45.0 million and cash of $8.0 million. What is the value of its equity? (in $ millions)
options: $67.0 million
$75.0 million
$83.0 million
$157.0 million
questions.explanation: Equity = EV − Debt + Cash = 120.0 − 45.0 + 8.0 = $83.0 million. Subtracting cash too gives $67.0 million; adding debt gives $157.0 million; ignoring cash gives $75.0 million.

questions.stem: Tamarack Solar just generated FCF of $2.5 million. FCF is expected to grow 3% per year forever and the firm's discount rate is 9% per annum. What is its enterprise value? (in $ millions)
options: $21.46 million
$28.61 million
$41.67 million
$42.92 million
questions.explanation: EV = FCF1/(R − g) = 2.5 × 1.03/(0.09 − 0.03) = 2.575/0.06 = $42.92 million. Using FCF0 gives $41.67 million; adding g to R gives $21.46 million; dividing by R alone gives $28.61 million.

questions.stem: Cascade Cabinetry's year shows (in $ millions): sales 48.0; cash operating costs 33.6; D&A 4.2; interest 1.5. The tax rate is 28%, CAPEX is 5.0 and ΔWC is 0.8. FCF is expected to stay constant forever and the firm's discount rate is 9% per annum. What is its enterprise value? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC

errors.label: Started from NPAT (after interest)
errors.explain: NPAT is after interest; FCF starts from EBIT(1 − T) so lenders' interest is not deducted.

errors.label: Subtracted interest from EBIT(1 − T)
errors.explain: Interest is a payment to a capital provider; FCF is the cash before those payments.

errors.label: Added CAPEX instead of subtracting
errors.explain: CAPEX is cash spent on assets, so it reduces FCF.
