questions.explanation: Income statement → EBIT → EBIT(1 − T) → FCF → EV. Interest never appears in FCF; it only matters later when debt is subtracted from EV to reach equity.

questions.stem: Laurentian Labs has constant FCF of $7.2 million per year forever and a discount rate of 8.5% per annum. It has debt of $24.0 million, cash of $3.5 million and 5.0 million shares. What is the equity value per share? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Subtracted cash as well as debt
errors.explain: Cash is added back: net debt = Debt − Cash.

errors.label: Divided EV by the share count
errors.explain: EV includes the lenders' claim; shareholders only own EV − Debt + Cash.

errors.label: Added debt and subtracted cash
errors.explain: That turns equity into something larger than EV; debt is a claim to subtract.

questions.explanation: Discounting FCF gives EV; per-share value requires moving from EV to equity and then dividing by shares.

questions.stem: Bow Valley Pipelines just produced FCF of $3.4 million, expected to grow 3.5% per year forever. The firm's discount rate is 9.5% per annum. What is its enterprise value? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Used FCF0 in the numerator
errors.explain: The growing perpetuity needs next year's FCF.

errors.label: Added g to R
errors.explain: The denominator is R − g.

errors.label: Divided by R alone
errors.explain: Growth lowers the capitalisation rate to R − g.

questions.explanation: FCF valuation uses exactly the same growing-perpetuity algebra as the Gordon model, with FCF in place of dividends and the firm's rate in place of the equity rate.

questions.stem: Whitecap Wind expects free cash flows of $2.0 million, $2.6 million and $3.1 million at the ends of years 1 to 3. From year 4 FCF grows 3% per year forever. The firm's discount rate is 10% per annum. What is its enterprise value today? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: Horizon value at year 3: EV3 = FCF4/(R − g)

errors.label: Used FCF3 instead of FCF4 in the horizon numerator
errors.explain: The horizon value needs the first constant-growth FCF, FCF4 = FCF3(1.03).

errors.label: Discounted FCF3 + EV3 four years
errors.explain: EV3 is a year-3 value: discount three periods.

errors.label: Left out FCF3
errors.explain: FCF3 is paid at year 3 along with EV3, which only covers year 4 onward.

questions.explanation: FCF valuation with a timeline is non-constant growth again: explicit flows, a horizon value at the date before constant growth begins, then discount everything.

questions.stem: Yukon Drillers earns EBIT of $12.0 million per year forever. A tax change lowers its tax rate from 30% to 26%; CAPEX equals D&A and ΔWC is zero. The firm's discount rate is 9% per annum. By how much does enterprise value rise? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Reported the annual FCF increase
errors.explain: A perpetual increase in FCF is capitalised at R: divide by 0.09.

errors.label: Used the new tax rate rather than the change
errors.explain: The change in T is 4 percentage points, not 26%.

errors.label: Capitalised the whole new FCF instead of the increase
errors.explain: That is the whole new FCF capitalised, not the increase.

questions.explanation: Because FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC, a cut in T raises FCF by EBIT × ΔT each year; the value created is that annual gain capitalised at R.

questions.stem: Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) is:
options: the cash generated by operations before any payment to lenders, EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
the dividends actually paid to shareholders during the year, as decided by the board
the cash available to shareholders after interest and net borrowing: NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
net income after tax, taken from the income statement without any adjustments
questions.explanation: FCFE is what shareholders could receive without hurting the business. It starts from NPAT (after interest), converts to cash with D&A, CAPEX and ΔWC, and adds net new borrowing. FCF (to the firm) is the pre-lender version; dividends are only what the board chooses to pay.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the FCFE formula?
options: NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC − ΔDebt
NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
questions.explanation: Net borrowing brings cash IN, so ΔDebt is added (and a repayment, a negative ΔDebt, reduces FCFE). Dropping it is the missing-delta-debt error; starting from EBIT(1 − T) is the FCF formula.

questions.stem: An analyst discounts forecast cash flows to shareholders, after interest and after net borrowing, at the cost of equity. The result is:
options: The equity value directly
Enterprise value (EV)
The value of the firm's debt
Book value of equity
questions.explanation: FCFE is the cash for shareholders, so its PV at the cost of equity is the equity value. No EV − Debt + Cash step is needed.

questions.stem: You want the equity value of a firm whose debt will rise and fall over the next five years. Which method fits best?
options: FCFE at the cost of equity, since it includes the planned borrowing and repayment
FCFF discounted at the cost of equity, since both are cash flows of the firm
FCFE discounted at the firm's overall rate, since the firm is what is being valued
The Gordon model with last year's FCFE as D1, since debt changes cancel out
questions.explanation: FCFE already contains ΔDebt, so it values the equity cash flows directly at the equity rate. Discounting FCFE at the firm rate (a lower figure) is a rate mismatch; FCFF is a firm-level cash flow and needs the firm rate.

questions.stem: How is FCFE related to FCF?
options: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt
FCFE = FCF + (1 − T) × Interest − ΔDebt
FCFE = FCF − Interest + ΔDebt, with interest before tax
FCFE = FCF, because interest is not a cash flow
questions.explanation: Going from the whole firm to equity holders, subtract the lenders' after-tax interest (interest saves tax, so only (1 − T) × Interest is lost) and add net new debt. Using pre-tax interest ignores the tax shield on interest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of FCFE?
options: It is discounted at the firm's overall discount rate to give enterprise value
It can exceed net income when the firm is borrowing
It includes interest because it starts from NPAT
Its present value at the cost of equity is the equity value
questions.explanation: FCFE is an equity-holder cash flow, discounted at the cost of equity to give equity. Enterprise value comes from discounting FCF at the firm's rate.

questions.stem: Why is ΔDebt added in FCFE?
options: New borrowing brings cash in for shareholders; repayments (negative ΔDebt) take cash away
Debt is an asset of the firm, so more debt directly increases the value of equity
Interest is only paid on new debt, so ΔDebt measures the interest bill
ΔDebt converts the book value of equity into its market value
questions.explanation: FCFE counts cash flows that equity holders can actually receive: operating cash after reinvestment, less what must go to lenders, plus new loans. If the firm repays $2 of principal, $2 less is available for shareholders.

questions.stem: A firm's FCFE this year is much larger than its NPAT, mainly because of a large increase in debt. How should an analyst read that?
options: The firm has become more profitable, and the extra cash will recur each year
The firm should cut its dividends to match FCFE and keep the difference
NPAT must have been understated by the accountants in the income statement
A one-off boost from borrowing; capitalising it would overstate equity value
questions.explanation: ΔDebt is cash from lenders, not earnings. A permanent perpetuity of FCFE that includes a big one-off ΔDebt overstates value; normalise borrowing before capitalising.

questions.stem: A firm reports (in $ thousands): NPAT 420; D&A 90; CAPEX 150; increase in working capital 20; net new borrowing 60. What is its FCFE?
options: $280 thousand
$310 thousand
$340 thousand
$400 thousand
questions.explanation: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt = 420 + 90 − 150 − 20 + 60 = 400. Leaving out net borrowing gives 340; subtracting it gives 280; forgetting the non-cash D&A add-back gives 310.

questions.stem: A firm has FCF of $5.8 million, interest of $0.9 million, a tax rate of 30%, and repays $1.2 million of debt during the year. What is its FCFE? (in $ millions)
options: $3.70 million
$3.97 million
$5.17 million
$6.37 million
questions.explanation: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt = 5.80 − 0.63 + (−1.20) = $3.97 million. Using pre-tax interest gives $3.70 million; treating the repayment as borrowing gives $6.37 million; omitting ΔDebt gives $5.17 million.

questions.stem: Prairie Grain Co-op has (in $ millions): sales 9.0; cash operating costs 5.4; D&A 0.9; interest 0.45; tax rate 30%; CAPEX 1.1; ΔWC 0.2; net new borrowing 0.5. FCFE is expected to stay constant forever. The firm's overall discount rate is 8% and shareholders require 11% per annum. What is the equity value? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt

solution: Equity = FCFE/R_E = 1.675/0.11 = $15.23 million (the 8% firm rate is not used for FCFE)

errors.label: Left out net new borrowing
errors.explain: New borrowing adds cash for shareholders and belongs in FCFE.

errors.label: Discounted FCFE at the firm's 8% rate
errors.explain: Equity cash flows carry the cost of equity (11%); 8% is the rate for FCF.

errors.label: Used FCF (before interest and borrowing) instead of FCFE
errors.explain: FCF is the whole-firm cash flow; shareholders get FCFE.

questions.explanation: Income statement → NPAT → FCFE → equity at the cost of equity. Interest is deducted here (via NPAT), and net borrowing is added.

questions.stem: Chinook Chemicals has EBIT of $6.0 million, a tax rate of 25%, D&A of $1.4 million, CAPEX of $2.0 million and ΔWC of $0.3 million. It pays interest of $0.8 million and repays $0.6 million of debt during the year. What is its FCFE? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC

errors.label: Subtracted pre-tax interest
errors.explain: Interest is tax-deductible, so the cost to shareholders is (1 − T) × Interest.

errors.label: Added the repayment instead of subtracting
errors.explain: A debt repayment is a negative ΔDebt and reduces FCFE.

errors.label: Left out ΔDebt
errors.explain: Net borrowing (here negative) must be added.

questions.explanation: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt is the bridge between the two cash flows. Here the firm both pays interest and shrinks its debt, so shareholders receive $1.2 million less than FCF.

questions.stem: Rideau Rail just generated FCFE of $4.2 million, expected to grow 4% per year forever. Shareholders require 10.5% per annum, the firm's overall discount rate is 8%, and there are 8.0 million shares. What is the equity value per share? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Used FCFE0 in the numerator
errors.explain: The growing perpetuity needs next year's FCFE.

errors.label: Discounted at the firm's 8% rate
errors.explain: FCFE is an equity cash flow and takes the cost of equity.

errors.label: Forgot to divide by the number of shares
errors.explain: 67.20 is the total equity value in $ millions.

questions.explanation: FCFE valuation is Gordon growth applied to cash flows to equity at R_E. Dividing by shares at the end gives the price per share.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards has NPAT of $1.6 million, D&A of $0.7 million, CAPEX of $1.2 million and ΔWC of $0.15 million. It wants FCFE of $2.0 million to fund a special payout to shareholders. How much net new debt must it raise? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: Required ΔDebt = target FCFE − FCFE before borrowing

errors.label: Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: ΔDebt must make up the SHORTFALL: target minus what operations already provide.

errors.label: Added ΔWC instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: An increase in working capital ties up cash and reduces FCFE.

errors.label: Forgot to add back D&A
errors.explain: D&A is a non-cash charge in NPAT and is added back.

questions.explanation: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt, rearranged for ΔDebt. Borrowing is the plug that closes the gap between operating cash and the payout target.

questions.stem: In the course's notation, working capital (WC) is:
options: Cash + Inventory + Receivables − Payables, i.e. current assets − current liabilities
Inventory + Receivables only, because cash is not an operating asset
Cash + Inventory + Receivables + Payables, the sum of the current items
Long-term assets minus long-term debt on the balance sheet
questions.explanation: WC = Cash + Inventory + Accounts Receivable − Accounts Payable = Current assets − Current liabilities. Payables are a liability, so they reduce WC. ΔWC is the CHANGE in this figure from one year to the next.

questions.stem: A retailer builds up inventory before the holiday season and pays for it in cash. In the FCF formula this shows up as:
options: A negative ΔWC, which raises FCF
A positive ΔWC, which reduces FCF
Higher CAPEX, which reduces FCF
Higher D&A, which raises FCF
questions.explanation: Inventory is part of WC, so more inventory means WC and ΔWC rise. A positive ΔWC is cash tied up in the business and is subtracted in FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC.

questions.stem: A company's suppliers agree to wait 15 more days for payment. Holding everything else constant, what happens to ΔWC and FCF this year?
options: Payables rise, so ΔWC rises as well and FCF falls by the increase in payables
Payables rise, so ΔWC falls (is negative) and FCF rises by that amount
Nothing happens, because payables are not part of working capital in this course
Payables rise, so CAPEX falls and FCF rises by the amount of the increase
questions.explanation: Payables are subtracted in WC. When they rise, WC falls and ΔWC < 0; subtracting a negative ΔWC in FCF adds cash. The firm is effectively borrowing from suppliers.

questions.stem: How do the level of working capital (WC) and the change in working capital (ΔWC) differ in a free cash flow calculation?
options: WC enters FCF each year, and ΔWC is only a memo item with no effect on cash flow
ΔWC is the sum of cash and receivables, and WC is the sum of inventory and payables
WC is a level at a date; only the yearly change ΔWC = WC_end − WC_start enters FCF
They are the same thing because working capital is already a flow, not a level
questions.explanation: FCF is a flow for one period, so it needs the change in WC over that period. Subtracting the whole WC level would charge the firm again every year for the same inventory and receivables.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT cause a positive change in working capital (ΔWC > 0) in a year?
options: An increase in inventory
An increase in accounts receivable
An increase in the cash balance
An increase in accounts payable
questions.explanation: Inventory, receivables and cash are positive items in WC, so an increase in any of them raises WC. Payables are subtracted, so higher payables lower WC. (The professor's list of positive ΔWC examples: inventory up, receivables up, payables down, cash up.)

questions.stem: Why does an increase in inventory reduce free cash flow even though inventory is an asset the firm owns?
options: The firm paid cash for goods it has not yet sold, so cash is tied up
Inventory is a liability on the balance sheet, so it reduces cash flow
Inventory is expensed immediately for tax purposes, lowering cash flow
Inventory raises D&A, and D&A reduces FCF dollar for dollar
questions.explanation: FCF counts cash, not assets. Buying inventory consumes cash now and returns it only when the goods are sold. The same logic applies to receivables (sales not yet collected).

questions.stem: A mature manufacturer collects receivables faster and trims inventory, so its working capital falls by $2 million this year while EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX is $10 million. What is this year's FCF, and is it sustainable?
options: FCF = $12 million; the extra $2 million is a one-off release of working capital
FCF = $8 million, because ΔWC is subtracted as an outflow
FCF = $10 million, because working capital does not affect FCF
FCF = $12 million and the $2 million will recur every year
questions.explanation: ΔWC = −2, so FCF = 10 − (−2) = $12 million. Releasing working capital is a one-time gain; capitalising it forever would overstate the firm's value.

questions.stem: True or false: ΔWC equals working capital at the end of the year minus working capital at the start of the year, and a positive ΔWC reduces FCF.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. ΔWC = WC_end − WC_start. FCF subtracts ΔWC, so cash tied up (ΔWC > 0) lowers FCF and cash released (ΔWC < 0) raises it.

questions.stem: During the year a firm's inventory rises by 55, receivables fall by 20, payables fall by 15 and cash rises by 10 (all in $ thousands). What is ΔWC?
options: $30 thousand
$50 thousand
$60 thousand
$100 thousand
questions.explanation: ΔWC = ΔCash + ΔInventory + ΔReceivables − ΔPayables = 10 + 55 + (−20) − (−15) = 60. A fall in payables RAISES WC. Treating the payables fall as a decrease gives 30; leaving out cash gives 50; treating the receivables fall as a rise gives 100.

questions.stem: A firm's current assets rise from 612 to 655 and its current liabilities fall from 340 to 312 (in $ thousands). What is ΔWC?
options: -$28 thousand
$15 thousand
$71 thousand
$343 thousand
questions.explanation: WC = current assets − current liabilities: 272 at the start, 343 at the end, so ΔWC = 343 − 272 = 71. Adding the change in liabilities instead of subtracting it gives 15; the ending level is 343; looking at liabilities alone gives −28.

questions.stem: Foothills Robotics's balance sheet shows (in $ thousands) at the start and end of the year: cash 120 and 150; inventory 310 and 365; receivables 240 and 262; payables 205 and 248. What is ΔWC? (Answer in $ thousands.)
solution: ΔWC = 529 − 465 = 64 (positive: cash tied up, FCF falls by 64)

errors.label: Added the payables
errors.explain: Payables are subtracted in working capital.

errors.label: Left out cash
errors.explain: In the course's definition cash is part of WC.

errors.label: Reported the ending WC
errors.explain: The question asks for the change over the year.

questions.explanation: Compute WC at both dates, then take the difference. Cash, inventory and receivables push WC up; payables pull it down.

questions.stem: Kootenay Kayaks has EBIT of 410, a tax rate of 30%, D&A of 95 and CAPEX of 120 (all in $ thousands). Current assets rose from 840 to 905 and current liabilities rose from 515 to 598. What is its free cash flow? (Answer in $ thousands.)

steps.label: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC

errors.label: Subtracted 18 instead of adding it back
errors.explain: ΔWC is negative (working capital fell), so subtracting it adds 18 to FCF.

errors.label: Left ΔWC out of the calculation
errors.explain: ΔWC belongs in FCF; here it releases 18 of cash.

errors.label: Subtracted the ending WC level
errors.explain: Only the CHANGE in WC enters FCF.

questions.explanation: Liabilities grew faster than assets, so working capital fell: the business was financed partly by its suppliers and FCF is higher than the pre-WC figure.

questions.stem: Gatineau Glass's annual cost of goods sold is $36.5 million. It negotiates to pay suppliers 10 days later, so payables rise by 10 days of cost of goods sold (use 365 days). By how much does this one-time change raise FCF this year? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Treated higher payables as an outflow
errors.explain: More payables lower WC, which raises FCF.

errors.label: Used 10% of COGS
errors.explain: 10 days is 10/365 of annual COGS (2.7%), not 10%.

errors.label: Counted the gain every year
errors.explain: The stretch is a one-off release, not a permanent annual gain.

questions.explanation: Stretching payables is cash borrowed from suppliers: ΔWC falls and FCF rises once. It cannot be repeated each year unless terms are stretched again.

questions.stem: Harbourfront Bakeries expects inventory to rise 40% from $1.25 million, receivables to rise 8% from $0.90 million, and payables to rise 15% from $0.60 million. Cash is unchanged. What is the expected ΔWC? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Added the payables increase
errors.explain: Payables are subtracted: more payables offset part of the inventory build.

errors.label: Counted inventory only
errors.explain: Receivables and payables also change.

errors.label: Used the ending levels instead of the changes
errors.explain: WC at the end is a level; ΔWC needs the differences.

questions.explanation: Each item's change is level × growth rate. Inventory and receivables increase WC; the payables increase offsets part of it.

questions.stem: The comparables approach to valuation:
options: discounts forecast dividends at the required return to obtain the price today
applies the multiple of similar firms (P/E, P/S, EV/EBITDA) to the target's earnings, sales or EBITDA
discounts free cash flows at the firm's overall discount rate to obtain EV
adds up the values of the firm's assets as if they were sold off in liquidation
questions.explanation: Comparables need no forecast of future cash flows: price = benchmark multiple × the firm's own metric. The other three descriptions are the DDM, FCFF valuation and liquidation value.

questions.stem: A regulated electric utility has paid steadily growing dividends for decades, and its payout policy is stable. Which method is the most natural way to value its shares?
options: Free cash flow to the firm, discounted at the cost of equity
Price/sales comparables, because dividends are not reliable
NPVGO, because the firm has no growth opportunities
The dividend discount model (Gordon growth)
questions.explanation: Stable, predictable dividends are exactly the condition under which the DDM works well. FCFF discounted at the cost of equity mixes the wrong rate with a firm-level cash flow, and price/sales is a fallback for firms without earnings.

questions.stem: Pathfinder Fibre pays no dividends and plans to borrow heavily to finance a network build-out over the next five years. You want the value of its shares directly from forecasts of what shareholders could receive. Which method fits?
options: FCFE discounted at the cost of equity
The Gordon growth model with D0 = 0
FCFF discounted at the cost of equity
A trailing P/E applied to this year's earnings
questions.explanation: With no dividends the DDM has nothing to discount until payouts begin, and FCFE captures both the heavy reinvestment and the planned borrowing. FCFF would give enterprise value (and needs the firm's rate), and a trailing P/E ignores the build-out.

questions.stem: A buyer wants the value of a target's operations regardless of how the target is currently financed, because it will replace the capital structure after the takeover. Which approach fits best?
options: FCFE discounted at the cost of equity using current borrowing
The DDM using the target's current dividend and growth rate
The target's book value of equity from its balance sheet
FCFF at the firm's rate (EV), then Equity = EV − Debt + Cash
questions.explanation: FCF is independent of the financing mix (it is before interest and debt flows), so it values the operations whatever the debt level. Equity is then derived from EV with the current net debt.

questions.stem: How do FCFF and FCFE differ as valuation methods?
options: FCFF gives the value of equity, whereas FCFE gives the value of the whole firm
FCFF is discounted at the firm's rate to give EV; FCFE at the cost of equity to give equity directly
Both are discounted at the cost of equity, but FCFE is measured after taxes
FCFF is built from dividends, whereas FCFE is built from earnings
questions.explanation: FCFF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC belongs to all capital providers (EV, firm rate). FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt belongs to shareholders (equity, cost of equity).

questions.stem: A young software company has sales but negative earnings and pays no dividend. Peers trade at about 4 times sales. Which valuation is the most workable?
options: P/E comparables applied to this year's negative earnings per share
Price/sales comparables applied to the company's sales per share
The Gordon model using the dividend paid this year as D0
NPVGO using the no-growth value EPS1/R as the price
questions.explanation: A P/E on negative earnings is meaningless and the Gordon model has no dividend to grow; a sales multiple still produces a positive number (SM 8-12 values a firm at 4.3 × sales per share).

questions.stem: Why can the dividend discount model be a poor choice for a firm that retains most of its earnings?
options: Retained earnings are discounted at a higher rate than paid-out dividends are
The DDM cannot be used at all whenever ROE is above the required return
Firms that retain earnings have no required return on their shares
Dividends then say little about the cash the business generates, so they understate its value
questions.explanation: The DDM values only cash paid out. If a firm reinvests most of its cash, current dividends are small or zero and say little about the value of the business; FCFE or FCFF capture the cash generated whether or not it is paid out.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason to prefer comparables over DCF methods?
options: They are quick and use observable market multiples
They avoid having to estimate a long-run growth rate and discount rate
They work for firms whose future cash flows are hard to forecast
Comparables require a detailed forecast of each future year's cash flows
questions.explanation: Comparables rely on peers' multiples applied to current or next-year earnings, sales or EBITDA. The cost is the benchmark: peers must really have similar g, ROE and R (SM 8 CTQ 12). A detailed multi-year forecast is the DCF's demand, not comparables'.

questions.stem: For a growing firm that pays no dividend, the DDM gives $22 per share while peers' P/E multiples imply $35. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The peers' P/E multiples must be wrong, because the DDM is the more reliable method
The firm is certainly overvalued at $35, because the DDM value is lower
The DDM is likely unsuitable: tiny dividends hide the cash flows; cross-check with FCFE or FCFF
The two methods must always agree, so there must be an arithmetic mistake
questions.explanation: When payouts are small, the DDM can understate value; the methods differ because their assumptions differ. A cash-flow model (FCFE/FCFF) fills the gap, and then you compare it with the comparables value.

questions.stem: True or false: if you discount FCFF at the firm's discount rate, you must still subtract debt and add cash to reach the value of the shares.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. FCFF discounted gives enterprise value. Equity = EV − Debt + Cash. By contrast, FCFE discounted at the cost of equity gives equity directly.

questions.stem: To value a firm's operations independently of how they are financed, discount _____ at the firm's overall discount rate.
options: free cash flow to the firm (FCF)
free cash flow to equity (FCFE)
dividends per share
net income after tax
questions.explanation: FCF is before payments to lenders and shareholders, so it is independent of the financing mix; its PV at the firm's rate is enterprise value.

questions.stem: Two analysts value the same firm. One discounts FCF at the firm's rate and computes Equity = EV − Debt + Cash; the other discounts FCFE at the cost of equity. Their equity values differ. What is the most likely reason?
options: Their forecasts or rates are inconsistent; built consistently, the two methods should agree
FCFF always gives a higher answer than FCFE, so the gap is expected
The DDM must be used to break the tie, since it is the only exact method
FCFE should be discounted at the firm's rate to make the two agree
questions.explanation: In theory both approaches describe the same business and should give the same equity value. A gap points to inconsistent assumptions, not to a rule that one method is higher. Discounting FCFE at the firm's rate would make a rate mismatch, not fix one.

questions.stem: An efficient market is one in which:
options: security prices never change, because all information is already known
every investor earns the same return on every security held
security prices reflect the relevant information, so securities are fairly priced
security prices always equal the book value per share on the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Efficiency is about information: if the relevant information is already in the price, there is no reason to think the price is too high or too low. Prices still move, because new information arrives constantly.

questions.stem: Weak-form market efficiency says that current prices already reflect:
options: all publicly released information, including financial statements
all information, including private information held by insiders
only the information in the firm's most recent earnings announcement
the past history of the stock's own prices (so charts cannot predict)
questions.explanation: Weak form is the mildest: the information set is the stock's past price history. If it holds, 'only the current price is important' and the path that led to it is irrelevant (L04 s47).

questions.stem: Which form of market efficiency says that prices reflect all publicly released information?
options: Weak form
Strong form
Perfect form
Semi-strong form
questions.explanation: Semi-strong adds public information (financial statements, announcements, news) to the past price history. Strong form adds private information too.

questions.stem: A technical analyst studies price charts for ten years and cannot beat a buy-and-hold strategy after costs. Which form of efficiency is this consistent with?
options: Weak-form efficiency
Strong-form efficiency only
The market being inefficient in every form
Semi-strong efficiency only, not weak
questions.explanation: If past prices carry no exploitable information, chart reading cannot earn abnormal profits: that is the weak-form hypothesis. Note that semi-strong efficiency implies weak form, so 'semi-strong only, not weak' is impossible.

questions.stem: How do the weak and semi-strong forms of efficiency differ?
options: Weak form covers public information and semi-strong covers private information
They cover the same information, but semi-strong also applies to bonds
Semi-strong includes weak form (past prices) plus all other public information, so it is stronger
Weak form is a stronger claim than semi-strong because it applies to all stocks
questions.explanation: The forms are nested: weak ⊂ semi-strong ⊂ strong. The information sets are past prices; all public information; all information including private.

questions.stem: According to the course, which forms of market efficiency do we want and which do we not want?
options: We want strong-form efficiency most; weak and semi-strong forms are undesirable
We want all three forms equally, since each prices in more information
We want weak form only; semi-strong and strong forms are undesirable
We want weak and semi-strong efficiency; strong-form efficiency is undesirable
questions.explanation: Weak and semi-strong efficiency mean prices quickly absorb past and public information, which is good for fair trading. Strong form would mean even private information is already in prices, which could only happen through insider trading.

questions.stem: Why is strong-form efficiency regarded as undesirable?
options: Strong-form efficiency makes prices far more volatile than investors want
Private information could be in prices only if insiders traded on it, which is illegal and unfair
It prevents the market from absorbing public information quickly
It requires investors to hold only index funds, removing choice
questions.explanation: In a healthy market, insiders should not be able to profit from non-public information, so prices should NOT reflect it before it is released. Strong-form efficiency would imply that insider trading is rampant (L04 s50).

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT implied by weak-form efficiency alone?
options: Chart patterns in past prices cannot predict future returns
Analysis of public financial statements cannot earn abnormal returns
The current price is the only price information that matters
A momentum strategy cannot earn abnormal returns
questions.explanation: Weak form concerns past prices only. Whether financial statements are already priced is the semi-strong question, so weak form alone does not rule out profits from public statement analysis.

questions.stem: A market is semi-strong form efficient. A listed firm unexpectedly announces earnings far above forecasts at 9:00 a.m. What should happen to the share price?
options: It jumps to the new fair level almost at once, with no tendency to drift afterwards
It rises gradually over the following eight days as investors catch up
It overshoots the fair level and then falls back over the next few days
It does not change, because earnings are already known to investors
questions.explanation: Semi-strong efficiency means public news is priced quickly and correctly: an immediate one-step adjustment. A gradual rise is a delayed reaction and an overshoot-and-correct path is an overreaction; both are inefficient (TB Fig 12.14).

questions.stem: F-Stop Camera's shares trade at $140 until the company announces a secret R&D success worth $40 per share. At the announcement the price jumps to $180 and stays there. What does this pattern show?
options: Strong-form efficiency, because the price reached the right level after the news
The market is not even weak-form efficient, because the price changed
The market is inefficient, because efficient prices should never jump
Consistent with semi-strong efficiency, but not strong form: the private news was not in the $140 price
questions.explanation: A single jump on announcement is the efficient response to public news. But before the announcement the price did not contain the private information (the existence of the system), so strong form does not hold. Prices SHOULD move when information arrives.

questions.stem: True or false: if a market is semi-strong form efficient, it must also be weak-form efficient.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Historical prices are public information, so any market whose prices reflect all public information also reflects past prices. The forms are nested (SM 12 CTQ 6).

questions.stem: True or false: if a market is weak-form efficient, it must also be semi-strong form efficient.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Weak form only says past prices are already reflected. Prices could still be slow to react to announcements and financial statements, which would make the market weak-form efficient but not semi-strong efficient.

questions.stem: The past history of prices is the information set for the _____ form of market efficiency.
options: semi-strong
strong
technical
weak
questions.explanation: Weak form: past prices (charting). Semi-strong: all public information. Strong: all information including private.

questions.stem: Why are all investments in an efficient market zero-NPV investments?
options: Efficient markets prevent firms from ever earning a profit on their investments
Competition drives the required return on every security down to zero
Efficient markets set every price equal to the book value of the asset
Prices are neither too high nor too low, so market value equals cost: investors get what they pay for
questions.explanation: NPV = value − cost. If price equals value because all relevant information is priced, the difference is zero. Investors still earn the required return for the risk taken; they just cannot expect more.

questions.stem: Order the forms of market efficiency from the smallest information set to the largest.
options: Weak, then semi-strong, then strong
Semi-strong, then weak, then strong
Strong, then semi-strong, then weak
Weak, then strong, then semi-strong
questions.explanation: Weak form covers past prices only; semi-strong adds all other public information; strong adds private information as well. Each claim contains the one before it.

questions.stem: An analyst consistently earns abnormal returns using only published financial statements, and this is widely documented. Which statement follows?
options: The market is not weak-form efficient, so semi-strong efficiency must fail too
The market is strong-form efficient, since all information is in the price
Nothing follows, because published financial statements are private information
The market is not semi-strong efficient (so not strong either); weak form could still hold
questions.explanation: Published statements are public information. Profiting from them contradicts semi-strong efficiency, which in turn contradicts strong form (nested). Weak form concerns only past prices and may still be true.

questions.stem: True or false: if prices fluctuate from day to day, the market cannot be efficient.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Prices change because new information keeps arriving, which is what an efficient market does; an absence of price movement in a fast-changing world would suggest inefficiency (TB 12.6).

questions.stem: If you decide to buy a stock because its price has continued to move upwards with momentum, then you are relying upon:
options: Weak-form inefficiencies
Weak form efficiency
Semi-strong form efficiency
Semi-strong form inefficiencies
None of the above
questions.explanation: Momentum means a past price trend predicts the subsequent movement. Using past prices to forecast is only profitable if prices are predictable from their own history, i.e. the market is NOT weak-form efficient: you rely on a weak-form inefficiency. Weak-form efficiency would say the trend carries no information, and semi-strong forms concern public announcements, not past price trends.

questions.stem: The momentum effect is the tendency for:
options: a stock that has risen sharply to fall back toward its starting price
all stocks to move in the same direction on the same trading day
a stock that has recently risen (fallen) to keep rising (falling), as past trends predict
stock prices to equal the discounted value of all future dividends
questions.explanation: Momentum is a counter-example to weak-form efficiency: if the past trend predicts the next move, prices are predictable from their own history and an inefficiency exists (L04 s47).

questions.stem: A fund buys stocks that rose over the past six months and sells those that fell. The fund is trying to profit from:
options: A semi-strong inefficiency (delayed reaction to news)
Strong-form efficiency
A weak-form inefficiency (momentum)
Differences in the required return R
questions.explanation: The trading rule uses only past prices, so the information it exploits is the price history. It makes money only if the market is not weak-form efficient.

questions.stem: Silver Birch Mining announces a large discovery. Its share price rises 5% on the day and then creeps up another 8% over the next eight trading days. This price path shows:
options: An efficient reaction, because the price rose
An overreaction, because the price rose by more than the news justified
A weak-form efficiency test, because only past prices matter
A delayed reaction, a semi-strong inefficiency: the news was not fully priced at once
questions.explanation: In a semi-strong efficient market the full adjustment happens at the announcement. A partial jump followed by drift means public information is priced slowly; buying right after the announcement would earn abnormal returns (TB Fig 12.14, broken line).

questions.stem: How do a delayed reaction and an overreaction to news differ, and what would you do in each case?
options: Delayed: the price adjusts only partly, then drifts to fair value, so trade after the news. Overreaction: it overshoots, then corrects, so trade against the jump
Delayed: the price overshoots the fair value and then corrects; overreaction: the price adjusts too slowly; trade with the initial move in both cases
Both are efficient reactions to public news, so neither one can be exploited profitably by anyone trading after the announcement
Delayed: no tendency to keep moving after the news; overreaction: the price stays at its new level afterwards for good
questions.explanation: Both are paths in an inefficient market. The delayed-reaction path (broken line in TB Fig 12.14) is below the fair price for days after good news; the overreaction path (dotted) overshoots and then falls back to the fair price.

questions.stem: Good news pushes a stock from $140 to $220 on day 0, but analysts agree the news is worth $40 per share (fair price $180). If the market overreacts and then corrects, what trade makes money?
options: Buy the stock after the jump and hold it until it reaches $260 per share
Do nothing, because market prices cannot be wrong even briefly
Sell (or short) after the jump, then buy back as the price falls toward $180
Buy the stock only before the announcement, then sell it on day 0
questions.explanation: The price is $40 above fair value after the overshoot. Selling at $220 and repurchasing near $180 profits as the correction happens. This is only possible if the market is NOT semi-strong efficient.

questions.stem: Why do profit opportunities from an inefficiency tend to shrink once many investors discover them?
options: Regulators ban the trading strategy once it becomes well known
The required return on the stock rises when many investors trade it
Competition: traders pushing the price toward fair value remove the opportunity
Companies change their reported earnings to remove the pattern
questions.explanation: Efficiency is created by competition among investors looking for mispriced stocks. As more of them exploit a pattern, price pressure removes it, so only small and uncommon inefficiencies survive (TB 12.6).

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT rely on a market inefficiency to make money?
options: Buying recent winners because past price trends persist
Holding a diversified portfolio to earn the market's required return for its risk
Buying immediately after good public news because prices adjust slowly
Selling a stock that has overshot after an announcement, expecting it to fall back
questions.explanation: Earning the required return for bearing risk needs no mispricing. The other three strategies profit only if prices are predictable (weak-form inefficiency) or react wrongly to public news (semi-strong inefficiency).

questions.stem: In a semi-strong efficient market, what return should an investor expect from buying a stock just after a public announcement?
options: An abnormal profit, because the news is good and positive for the firm
A loss, because the price has already moved before the investor could trade
A return equal to the risk-free rate regardless of the stock's risk
Only the return that compensates for the risk; the trade has zero NPV
questions.explanation: News is already in the price by the time you can trade, so the purchase is fairly priced: NPV = 0. You still earn the required return for the risk taken, but no abnormal return.

questions.stem: True or false: a momentum strategy can earn abnormal profits only if the market is not weak-form efficient.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Momentum uses past prices only. If the market were weak-form efficient, the price history would carry no predictive information and the strategy could not beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis.

questions.stem: A market is semi-strong form efficient but not strong-form efficient. Which investor could still earn abnormal profits (ignoring the law)?
options: One who trades on published financial statements
One who studies price charts
One who trades on private information before it is announced
One who buys immediately after a press release
questions.explanation: Semi-strong efficiency prices past prices and all public information. Private information is not yet in prices, so trading on it can pay, which is why insider trading is prohibited (SM 12 CTQ 10c).

questions.stem: Why would chart reading (technical analysis) fail to beat the market if the market is weak-form efficient?
options: Charts are too expensive to produce compared with the profits available
Technical analysts cannot read financial statements or earnings reports
The current price already reflects the whole price history, so patterns carry no information
Weak-form efficiency means prices follow a perfectly predictable pattern
questions.explanation: In a weak-form efficient market the current price already embeds the past price history. 'Only the current price is important. The past history of how it got there is irrelevant' (L04 s47).

questions.stem: A stock trades at $140. News arrives showing it is worth $180, but on the announcement day the price rises only to $160, and over the next eight days it drifts up to $180. You buy at $160 on the announcement day and sell at $180 eight days later. Ignoring costs and the required return over eight days, what is your return on this trade? (Answer in %.)

steps.label: Profit per share = sale price − purchase price

errors.label: Measured the gain against the pre-news price of $140
errors.explain: Your cost was $160, the price you actually paid.

errors.label: Measured the gain against the sale price
errors.explain: A return is profit divided by the amount invested at the start.

errors.label: Used the full $40 revaluation as the profit
errors.explain: Part of the $40 jump ($20) happened before you could trade, so only $20 is available to you.

questions.explanation: A delayed reaction leaves a profit for those who trade right after the news; in an efficient market the price would have jumped to $180 immediately and the trade would earn nothing abnormal.

questions.stem: After a good-news announcement a stock's price rises to $215, then falls steadily back to $180 over the next two weeks, where the fair value was estimated to be. Which conclusion is best?
options: The market is semi-strong efficient, because the price ended at the right level
The market overreacted and then corrected: a trader could profit by selling after the jump
The market is weak-form efficient, because the price returned to fair value
The news must have been wrong, because the price fell after the announcement
questions.explanation: An efficient market goes straight to the fair price on the news. Overshoot-and-correct means the price was wrong for days, which is an inefficiency (semi-strong); ending at the right level does not make the path efficient.

questions.stem: Noise trading is trading:
options: based on private information about the firm's future earnings and dividends
driven by reasons unrelated to information about value, such as a health expense or a tax bill
carried out only by professional market makers who quote bid and ask prices
that follows chart patterns in the stock's past prices to forecast moves
questions.explanation: Noise traders buy or sell for personal or liquidity reasons (health, taxes, bills due), not because they have analysed value. Their trades can push prices away from fair value for a while (L04 s51).

questions.stem: The disposition effect is the tendency of investors to:
options: buy stocks only after they have fallen
sell all stocks at the end of the tax year
sell winning stocks too early and hold losing stocks too long
hold diversified portfolios regardless of price
questions.explanation: The disposition effect is a behavioural bias: realising gains feels good and realising losses feels bad, so investors sell winners and keep losers regardless of the stocks' future prospects.

questions.stem: Early in April a retiree sells a block of shares she still likes in order to pay her income tax bill. This is an example of:
options: Noise trading
The disposition effect
Overconfidence
Momentum investing
questions.explanation: She is selling for a personal cash need (taxes due), not because she thinks the stock is overpriced. That is noise trading. The disposition effect would require selling because of gain/loss on the position.

questions.stem: An investor sells a stock that has doubled to 'lock in the gain' but keeps a stock that has lost 40%, saying 'I will sell when it gets back to what I paid.' This behaviour is:
options: Noise trading
The disposition effect
Sentiment
Weak-form efficiency
questions.explanation: Selling the winner and holding the loser, anchored on the purchase price, is the textbook disposition effect.

questions.stem: A day trader believes she can out-guess the market and trades several hundred times a month, even though her results are no better than the index. Which behavioural factor does this illustrate?
options: The disposition effect
Noise trading for tax reasons
Semi-strong efficiency
Overconfidence
questions.explanation: Overconfidence leads investors to overestimate their ability and trade too much. The excess trading costs money and adds noise to prices.

questions.stem: After a long bull market, a wave of optimism lifts the prices of many tech stocks well beyond what their earnings forecasts justify. This is best described as:
options: The disposition effect
Liquidity noise from tax selling
Sentiment among investors
Strong-form efficiency
questions.explanation: Sentiment is a shared mood (optimism or pessimism) that moves prices independently of fundamentals. It is one of the behavioural reasons prices may deviate from fair value.

questions.stem: How do noise trading and behavioural biases differ as reasons why prices may deviate from fair value?
options: Noise comes from personal or liquidity needs; behavioural biases are systematic psychological errors
Noise trading is illegal, whereas behavioural biases are legal, and only the first can move prices
Noise trading affects only bonds, whereas behavioural biases affect only stocks and no other securities
They are the same thing described with different names, so the distinction has no content
questions.explanation: The slide groups them as two sources of mispricing: Noise (selling for personal reasons such as health, selling when bills like tax are due) and Behaviour (disposition effect, overconfidence, sentiment).

questions.stem: Why can noise trading move a stock's price away from its fair value?
options: Noise traders always possess valuable private information about the firm
Noise trading changes the firm's future dividends and therefore its true value
The pressure has nothing to do with value, so it can push the price until others step in
Noise trading forces the firm to reissue its shares at lower prices
questions.explanation: Fair value comes from expected cash flows. A forced seller shifts supply without changing those cash flows, which temporarily lowers the price below value until buyers who notice the discount arrive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for price deviations listed in the course?
options: Selling for personal reasons such as health
Firms paying dividends at fixed dates every year
Selling when bills such as tax are due
Overconfidence and sentiment among investors
questions.explanation: The slide lists noise (personal and tax-driven selling) and behaviour (disposition effect, overconfidence, sentiment). A regular dividend calendar is not a source of mispricing.

questions.stem: Many investors sell losing stocks in late December to realise tax losses, pushing some prices below value with no news about the firms. What could a disciplined investor do?
options: Buy at the depressed price, expecting the discount to vanish when the selling ends
Sell the same stocks short to ride the decline caused by tax-loss selling
Avoid the stocks, because in an efficient market prices are always right
Wait for the next dividend payment before deciding whether to buy
questions.explanation: If price pressure comes from non-informational selling, the discount should reverse once it ends. Capturing it requires patience and capital, which is why such deviations can persist.

questions.stem: A stock falls 12% on heavy volume in the last week of December with no company news, then recovers most of the loss in January. Which explanation is most consistent with the course?
options: The market learned bad private information in December and good news in January
The market is strong-form efficient, so price changes without news are impossible
Tax-related noise selling pushed the price below fair value, and it recovered when the pressure ended
The dividend was cut in December and restored in January, moving the price
questions.explanation: A sharp fall with no news that reverses is the signature of non-informational selling (here, tax selling). An information-driven move would not reverse on its own.

questions.stem: True or false: selling a stock to pay for a medical bill, rather than because of a view about its value, is an example of noise trading.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The seller is motivated by a personal cash need (health), which is unrelated to information about the firm; the course lists 'selling for personal reasons such as health' as noise.

questions.stem: Investors who hold on to losing stocks while selling their winners are showing the _____ effect.
options: momentum
disposition
efficiency
dividend
questions.explanation: The disposition effect is the habit of selling winners and holding losers.
